episodes.summary: The lynching of Charles Pierce took place in Bloomington, McLean County, Illinois, on the night of October 1, 1881, when a crowd of about 5,000 broke into the county jail and hanged Pierce, a prisoner held for horse stealing, from a nearby tree. Earlier that evening Pierce had shot and killed the jailer, Ted Franks. Papers nationwide noted that "best citizens" led the mob, which blamed the courts for failing to punish murder.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Olson
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Thomas Olson was a mob threat against a 17-year-old Swedish laborer held in the jail at Aurora, Illinois, on October 2, 1881, after he was accused of fatally stabbing Otto Freese the night before. Officials removed Olson secretly while a crowd gathered, and a party of about 100 young men that set out on October 4 to lynch him turned back before reaching Geneva. The Chicago Tribune covered the case beside its report of a lynching at Bloomington, and a short wire item ran across the upper Midwest.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Tom Herbert
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Tom Herbert was an attack by a mob on the jail at Kernville, Kern County, California, on the night of October 18, 1881, intended to seize and hang Herbert, a prisoner charged with murdering the mine owner who had employed him. Deputy Sheriff Ben Mitchell, who met the mob short of the jail, was shot dead, and his return fire wounded one of the attackers, Jim Cochran. The mob dispersed without reaching Herbert, and Bakersfield dispatches carried the story as far as Chicago and Memphis.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jacob Whitmore
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Jacob Whitmore occurred at Bellefontaine, Ohio, in early October 1881, when crowds gathered to hang Whitmore, a young farmer jailed on the charge of poisoning his wife. Sheriff H. M. Cline took him to a neighboring county before the crowd could act, and militia guarded the jail through the night. Whitmore was later indicted for first-degree murder; no paper gives the race of anyone involved.

episodes.title: Sharkey County ambush of 1881
episodes.summary: The Sharkey County ambush of 1881 was the shooting of a body of Black men on their way to a Fusion political meeting in Sharkey County, Mississippi, on the night of October 28, 1881, by men hidden beside the road. Perry Thompson was killed instantly, and later accounts said two of the wounded also died. The shooters were not identified, and Mississippi papers of both parties condemned the killing as a political assassination tied to a bitter contest over county offices.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Jones
episodes.summary: The lynching of Charles Jones took place at Spadra, Johnson County, Arkansas, on Monday, October 31, 1881, when a mob took Jones, a Black man accused of attempting to rape a white woman, from an officer at the railroad depot and hanged him to a tree. Jones was hanged within twenty minutes of arriving at Spadra, after what the wire called a "short informal examination by a jury." A Little Rock dispatch carried the story across the country, where papers ran it under headlines such as "Speedy Justice" and "Judge Lynch's Court in Arkansas."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Boge Jackson and Henry Hill
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Boge Jackson and Henry Hill took place at Hamburg, Arkansas, on October 22, 1881, when a crowd of several thousand that had gathered to see the two Black men hanged learned that the governor had reprieved them. Many in the crowd wanted to lynch the prisoners, and one report said they were held back only with great effort, but no attack is reported. Hill's sentence was later commuted to life imprisonment, and Jackson was legally hanged at Hamburg on November 18.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank and John McDonald
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Frank and John McDonald was the killing of two cousins by a mob at Menominee, Michigan, on the night of September 27, 1881, after they had been jailed on a charge of fatally stabbing a young man named Willie Kittson. A crowd that reports put at 400 to more than 500 people overpowered the sheriff, broke into the county jail and dragged the two men to their deaths. Wire summaries carried the story across the country in early October, and a Wisconsin paper later reported the arrest of members of the lynching party.

episodes.title: Mendota mob threat against a burglar (1881)
episodes.summary: The Mendota mob threat against a burglar was an incident at Mendota, Illinois, reported in October 1881, in which a mob put a noose around the neck of a man accused of burglary and made him choose between hanging and promising to plead guilty. The man promised, and the mob dispersed without killing him. The story survives only as a short unattributed paragraph that newspapers ran with an ironic comment on the mob's idea of justice.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bob Williams
episodes.summary: The lynching of Bob Williams was the hanging of a Black man, also reported as Robert Williams, by a crowd of about one hundred men in the woods across the Saluda River from Pelzer, South Carolina, on November 4, 1881. Williams was accused of raping a nine-year-old white girl and was taken from the guard house at Williamston. A coroner's jury found death at the hands of unknown parties, though a dispatch said the lynchers did not hide their identity and the lynching was "highly commended."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Adrian, Illinois
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching at Adrian, Illinois, took place on November 9, 1881, when a mob at Adrian, in Hancock County, tried to seize a young Black farm hand from the officers bringing him back from Peoria and shot him three times. He had been accused of assaulting a farmer's wife, Mrs. Kenkel (also spelled Kunkel), and officers carried him under guard to the county jail at Carthage, where he was reported to be dying. Short wire accounts of the shooting ran in papers from Wisconsin to Mississippi and New Mexico over the next ten days.

episodes.title: Lynching of Chris Davis
episodes.summary: The lynching of Chris Davis took place in Athens, Ohio, on the night of November 20-21, 1881, when a mob took Davis, a Black man described as a "mulatto," from the county jail and hanged him from a Hocking River bridge. Davis was being held on a charge of raping and beating with an ax an elderly widow near Albany, Ohio. A coroner's jury blamed "parties unknown," Albany women endorsed the hanging, and papers North and South debated it.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ed Maxwell
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Ed Maxwell was the hanging of a prisoner, also called Ed Williams, by a crowd at the court house in Durand, Pepin County, Wisconsin, on Saturday afternoon, November 19, 1881. Accused with his brother Lon of killing the Coleman brothers the previous July, he was taken from the sheriff's officers at his preliminary examination and hanged from a tree in the court-house yard. The case drew national comment over a reported coroner's verdict that he had fallen down the court-house steps, a dispute over a reporter's account, and Southern retorts that lynching was not only Southern.

episodes.title: Lynching of Craig and Parker Jordan
episodes.summary: The lynching of Craig and Parker Jordan was the hanging of two Black men by a mob in Leflore County, Mississippi, on the night of November 26, 1881, after they were accused of assassinating Robert Catlin, a white man. Both were said to have confessed after their capture and were hanged to a tree near a place the dispatches called Shepherdstown. Wire stories carried the case across the country, and Mississippi papers greeted it as "speedy vengeance."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Robinson
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of William Robinson took place in Kanawha County, West Virginia, in November 1881, after Robinson was accused of shooting and killing Allen Belcher, the town marshal of Malden, on November 15. Telegraphic reports said a mob was coming or organizing to take Robinson from the Charleston jail and hang him, and guards, militia and federal marshals were posted around the jail. No attack on the jail was reported, and a Charleston correspondent wrote that no lynching had ever been planned.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ed Partridge
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Ed Partridge followed the death of his six-year-old stepdaughter, Bell Holmes, on a Georgia plantation near Americus in late October or early November 1881. A coroner's jury found that the girl died of beatings at Partridge's hands, and he escaped from custody before a New York wire dispatch reported that local citizens threatened to lynch him. No lynching or recapture appears in the coverage, which spread the case nationally as a brief item under headlines such as "A Georgia Brute."

episodes.title: Caperton Station shooting
episodes.summary: The Caperton Station shooting was the shooting of a Black striking miner named Lewis by J. W. St. Clair, the prosecuting attorney of Fayette County, West Virginia, at Caperton Station on the evening of November 1, 1881. St. Clair fired on Lewis as he tried to escape after his arrest, and the first dispatches reported him killed. Later reports said he had only been wounded, and one Washington paper questioned whether he had been shot for striking or for being Black.

episodes.title: Rockdale County posse killing (1881)
episodes.summary: The Rockdale County posse killing was the fatal shooting of an unnamed Black man by a posse in Rockdale County, Georgia, reported from Atlanta on November 23, 1881. The man, accused of robbing a store, was shot dead after he refused an order to stop, and a jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide. The brief dispatch ran in papers from Georgia to Texas and Pennsylvania, which headed it variously as a robber's death or as "justifiable homicide."

episodes.title: Lynching of James P. Holland
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of James P. Holland was the hanging of a prisoner accused of murder by masked men who broke into the jail at Dardanelle, Yell County, Arkansas, about midnight on November 26–27, 1881. Holland had escaped jail before a verdict in his trial for an 1879 killing and had been returned from Tennessee hours earlier; he was hanged in the jail yard where a mob had hanged a man named Taylor months before. Papers nationwide carried it as another Arkansas lynching, while a Russellville paper printed a letter defending it.

episodes.title: Masked-band attacks on Black residents of Kenton, Tennessee
episodes.summary: The masked-band attacks on Black residents of Kenton, Tennessee, were a series of raids in the autumn of 1881 in which masked men repeatedly entered the Obion County town and whipped and maltreated Black men, women and children. Residents appealed to the governor, and Governor Hawkins offered a $250 reward for the arrest and conviction of those responsible. Tennessee papers carried the raids as brief state-news items, and at least one Northern paper presented them as a remnant of the Ku Klux.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of J. M. Garrison
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of J. M. Garrison took place at Winfield, Du Page County, Illinois, in late November 1881, when farmers who supplied his cheese factory gathered with a rope to hang him after the factory burned. Garrison's creditors accused him of setting the fire to avoid paying them, but the county sheriff intervened and took him to jail at Wheaton. Chicago dispatches about his escape were reprinted under headings such as "Escaped Lynching" in papers from Delaware to Minnesota and Wisconsin.

episodes.title: Lynching of Massey Hill
episodes.summary: The lynching of Massey Hill took place on the night of Saturday, November 5, 1881, when a mob took Hill, a Black man, from the jail at Manchester, Tennessee, and killed him. Hill had been accused of attempting to rape a little girl near the town, and two papers reported that he was hanged. A one-sentence Nashville dispatch carried the news across the country, where it was often printed beside the lynching of Robert Williams in South Carolina the same week.

episodes.title: Killing of Robert Harvey
episodes.summary: The killing of Robert Harvey was the killing of a Black man by Sheriff Lewis of Austin County, Texas, reported in a telegram from Brenham dated November 28, 1881. The telegram said Harvey was killed while resisting arrest and described him as "a cow thief and a bad negro." The two-sentence report ran in Waco and Dallas papers and is the only account found.

episodes.title: Shooting of Manning Law
episodes.summary: The shooting of Manning Law was the pursuit and shooting of a Black man, Manning Law, by the two brothers of his white bride, Mary Lewis, in Lexington County, South Carolina, in late October 1881. Overtaken on the road soon after the wedding, Law fired at the brothers and was shot in the breast; one dispatch said he was killed, while fuller versions said he was mortally wounded and that it was not known whether he died. Papers from Illinois to Tennessee carried the story under headlines about "miscegenation", and one cited it as a case of "Judge Lynch".

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Rigney
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Charles Rigney took place at Rockville, Maryland, in November 1881, after Rigney, a young Black farm hand, was accused of assaulting the five-year-old daughter of a Montrose storekeeper. The girl's father beat him and, with four other men, bound him and delivered him to the county jail, and threats to take him out and lynch him were reported for two nights. No attack came; the grand jury indicted him for an attempt rather than rape, and papers reported that the danger of lynching had passed.

episodes.title: Whipping of Jordan Denny
episodes.summary: The whipping of Jordan Denny was a night attack on an elderly Black mail carrier at his home in Lancaster, Garrard County, Kentucky, in early November 1881, shortly before his planned wedding. Accounts disagree on the night, the attackers and his injuries, and papers in Kentucky, Texas and Utah all treated it as a comic item.

episodes.title: Killing of Felix Burke
episodes.summary: The killing of Felix Burke was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Deputy Sheriff McDonald in Monroe County, Arkansas, in early November 1881, while the deputy was trying to arrest him on a charge of stealing a mule. McDonald was badly wounded in the exchange of fire, and the episode reached distant newspapers only as a brief telegraphic crime item.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Madder
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Charles Madder was an attack by a mob of several hundred people on the jail at Tiffin, Ohio, early on November 7, 1881, in an effort to seize Madder, a Heidelberg College divinity student held on the charge of shooting Phoebe Bernard. The sheriff's armed posse drove the crowd off after a fight in which officers were injured, and Madder was moved secretly to Fremont and then to the Toledo jail. The repulse was carried by wire across the country, while a Tiffin dispatch in the paper of Madder's home county called the reports false.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Joe Smith
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Joe Smith took place at Weedsport, New York, on November 18, 1881, when a mob tried to take Smith, a prisoner accused of outraging and nearly murdering a young woman, from the constable who had brought him there. The constable held the mob off, and the sheriff and a posse kept guard over the prisoner, who "narrowly escaped lynching by the villagers." The episode ran as a short wire item in papers from Maine to Georgia and Tennessee; none of them stated Smith's race.

episodes.title: Marion election riot
episodes.summary: The Marion election riot was a shooting at the polls at Marion Station, Lauderdale County, Mississippi, on election day, November 8, 1881, followed that afternoon by a sheriff's posse's siege of the house of Ed Vance, a white Republican, where Black men had taken refuge. Four white men died of the shooting at the polls; at the house the posse killed Vance's son John, lost one of its own men and fired on fleeing Black men, with reports of Black dead ranging from none to fifteen. Wire reports blamed armed Black men, while Republican papers printed accounts in which white Democrats began the attack.

episodes.title: Marion election riot and Vance house siege
episodes.summary: The Marion election riot and Vance house siege was a pair of linked shootings on November 8, 1881, election day, at Marion Station in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, about five miles from Meridian. After four white men were killed or mortally wounded at the polls, a sheriff's posse of about 100 men besieged the house of Ed Vance, a white Republican, and killed his son John, while a posse member, A. G. Warren, was shot dead from the house. Wire reports blamed armed Black men and the Vances, but Republican correspondents later published a version in which white Democrats began the shooting.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sandy King and Russian Bill
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Sandy King and Russian Bill was the hanging of two men accused of stealing stock by over a dozen masked men at the jail in Shakespeare, New Mexico, at about 2 a.m. on November 9, 1881. The two, described as members of a "noted cowboy gang" held for trial, were hanged from a joist after the mob seized their guard. A Tucson dispatch carried the story to papers across the country within a day, while correspondents in New Mexico and Arizona wrote of the hanging with approval or mockery.

episodes.title: Coal Valley strike and Black replacement miners (1881)
episodes.summary: The Coal Valley strike and Black replacement miners episode was a confrontation in November 1881 in Fayette County, West Virginia, in which striking coal miners at Coal Valley drove off the first group of Black miners brought from Virginia to take their places. When a second group arrived, county authorities called for troops, and two militia companies guarded the new men until the strikers dispersed. Accounts in the Wheeling Register differed on whether the strikers used threats: a visiting correspondent said they stopped "short of violence," while the county prosecutor said they threatened the men's lives.

episodes.title: Lynching of Richard Jennings
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Richard Jennings took place at Austin, Nevada, early on December 14, 1881, when a party of masked men took him from the county jail and hanged him from the front of the Court-house. Jennings, a miner newly arrived from Grass Valley, California, had been jailed on a charge of shooting John A. Barrett, a well-liked Austin resident, on December 12. The story ran by wire across the country, and Nevada papers largely endorsed the hanging as a warning to armed roughs.

episodes.title: Anniston calaboose shooting
episodes.summary: The Anniston calaboose shooting was the killing of two Black men, named in the press only as Greenwood and Hammond, by the town marshal and his deputy at the lock-up in Anniston, Alabama, in late November or early December 1881. The officers fired when a crowd of Black men pressed them as they jailed a prisoner, and an inquest and a preliminary hearing cleared them. Newspapers across the country carried the story as a riot in 'a mining town' put down by police.

episodes.title: Shooting of Hampton Price
episodes.summary: The shooting of Hampton Price was the fatal shooting of a Black man described as a "negro conjurer and so called doctor" by Oliver, the town sergeant of Franklin, Southampton County, Virginia, in December 1881. According to the reports, Price struck the officer with a black-jack when the sergeant pressed him to return fifty cents paid for a charm, and Oliver shot him in the back as he fled. Oliver was charged with the shooting, and Virginia papers took note when both witnesses for the Commonwealth died within days, leaving the prosecution without evidence.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Brodie and Shadrack Hester
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Brodie and Shadrack Hester took place in the early hours of December 1, 1881, at Oxford, Granville County, North Carolina, when a party of masked men took the two Black prisoners from the county jail and hanged them. Both men were held on a charge of murdering Thomas M. Lynch, an Oxford jeweler, and had not been tried. The Raleigh wire carried the story nationally the same day, and several North Carolina papers presented the hanging as just retribution.

episodes.title: Killing of Isaac Hicks
episodes.summary: The killing of Isaac Hicks was the fatal shooting of a Black man by two Savannah policemen at a railway section camp outside Savannah, Georgia, in late December 1881, while they were searching for a different man. Hicks ran from a shanty when the officers came to the door, was shot in three places, and died the next morning at the police barracks. The Savannah Morning News headlined the case "The Wrong Man Killed," and under a coroner's jury's majority verdict the officers were held for the grand jury.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dave Bumpers
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Dave Bumpers was the hanging of a Black eighteen-year-old by a mob at Athens, Georgia, in mid-December 1881. Bumpers had been accused of assaulting Mrs. Driscoll in her home, and the mob took him from the officers holding him and hanged him to an oak tree with a plow line. Northern and Southern papers carried the news as a short wire item, several under headlines that called him a "brute" or a "miscreant."

episodes.title: Pratt coal mines arrest shooting
episodes.summary: The Pratt coal mines arrest shooting was the killing of an unnamed Black man by an officer at the Pratt coal mines in Jefferson County, Alabama, reported in a Montgomery dispatch of December 9, 1881. According to the dispatch, the man resisted arrest and took up a shotgun, and the officer shot him before he could fire. The item ran as a brief telegraphic crime notice in papers from Pennsylvania to Texas.

episodes.title: Sibley's Mill shootings
episodes.summary: The Sibley's Mill shootings were a pair of fatal shootings in Baldwin County, Alabama, opposite Mobile, in late December 1881, in which a deputy sheriff and an unnamed Black man accused of ambushing the deputy's brother shot each other during an arrest. Deputy Sheriff Abe Johnson died within fifteen minutes, and a crowd that set out after the wounded suspect found him dead near a swamp. A Mobile dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, several of which presented the suspect's death as swift vengeance.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of David McMillan
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of David McMillan took place at the jail in Greenfield, Massachusetts, on the evening of December 6, 1881, when a crowd tried to seize McMillan, who was accused of shooting the parish priest, Father McCarthy. Officers holding the prisoner displayed revolvers, the crowd fell back, and McMillan was lodged in jail unharmed. Wire reports of the scene, under headings such as "Fear of Lynching" and "Safe in Jail", ran in papers across the country.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of George Mills
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of George Mills took place at Hannibal, Missouri, in December 1881, when a posse of fifteen men who seized Mills on an accusation of attempted rape barely kept him from being lynched. Mills was handed over to the authorities, and the story ran as a short wire item in several out-of-state papers on December 21.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching at Lafayette, Alabama (1881)
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching at Lafayette, Alabama, took place in December 1881, when a crowd was reported going to the Lafayette jail to demand a Black prisoner accused of killing a merchant in Chambers County. A Montgomery dispatch said there was a "strong probability" that the man had been hanged, and papers from Savannah to Sacramento repeated the story, one of them as an accomplished lynching. No later report confirming or denying his death appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Allen
episodes.summary: The lynching of William Allen was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a party of masked men near Warwick Court House, Virginia, on the night of December 5, 1881. Allen had been jailed three days earlier, accused of fatally stabbing a white man, William S. Selater, near Newport News. The lynchers reportedly obtained him with a forged transfer order, and the one man arrested, a white barber named Thomas Valentine, was discharged for lack of evidence.

episodes.title: Disappearance and reported lynching of Mark Thompson
episodes.summary: The disappearance and reported lynching of Mark Thompson took place near Dawson, Georgia, in late November or early December 1881, when white men seized Thompson, a young Black man, as a suspect in an attack on a man named John E. Moreland and carried him away. He was reported beaten to death, but searchers found only a bloody shirt and socks buried in a swamp. A wire dispatch carried the story to papers from Pennsylvania to California, most of which headlined the robbery rather than the killing.

episodes.title: Death of an unidentified Black man near Reagan, Texas (1881)
episodes.summary: The death of an unidentified Black man near Reagan, Texas, came to light around Christmas 1881, when his body was found on a railroad track near the town after two trains had reportedly passed over it. The Waco Daily Examiner, the only paper found to report it, suggested that unknown persons had killed and robbed him and left his body on the track to hide the crime.

episodes.title: Mob hanging of Ilen Pettis
episodes.summary: The mob hanging of Ilen Pettis took place in White County, Arkansas, in late December 1881, when ten masked men took Pettis, a Black prisoner accused of robbery, from jail and hanged him from a tree limb until he confessed. The men returned him alive to the jailer and handed the recovered money to the sheriff. It is known only from one Chicago Tribune dispatch, which reported it approvingly.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Alonzo Garner
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Alonzo Garner took place in St. Paul, Minnesota, on Sunday night, December 18, 1881, when a crowd nearly lynched Garner after he was arrested on a charge of setting several fires near the Post Siding. Garner survived, was indicted for arson, and was convicted the next month of attempting to burn a store. The only report of the attempt on him was a single clause in the St. Paul Daily Globe's police-court column, and no paper gave his race.

episodes.title: Killing of Ed Nelms
episodes.summary: The killing of Ed Nelms was the fatal shooting of Ed Nelms, a Black man who had escaped from a Mississippi jail while under sentence of death, by Memphis Chief of Police W. C. Davis on the Arkansas bank of the Mississippi River opposite Memphis early on December 29, 1881. A coroner's jury at Memphis found the same day that Davis was "thoroughly justifiable." The Memphis dailies praised the chief at length, and a brief dispatch carried the story nationwide.

episodes.title: Lynching ruse against William Miller
episodes.summary: The lynching ruse against William Miller took place at the jail in Aberdeen, Mississippi, on the night of December 24, 1881, when Miller, a Black prisoner held as accomplice in a triple murder, was taken from his cell "under the threat and pretext of being lynched." The removal left his cellmate, the white suspect W. Robert Jones, alone to be questioned, and Jones confessed. Both men were convicted at a special term of court in January 1882 and sentenced to hang.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of George Berry
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of George Berry took place at Texarkana, Arkansas, on December 30, 1881, when railroad men took Berry from officers who were bringing him to jail and tried to hang him for the shooting of John Smith. The hanging failed because the cotton scales they used were too low, and the men handed Berry back to the officers while vowing to hang him if Smith died. The story ran by telegraph in papers from Richmond to Los Angeles, most of which predicted a lynching that night.

episodes.title: Police shooting of Sam Duckett
episodes.summary: The police shooting of Sam Duckett took place on Christmas afternoon, 25 December 1881, in South Washington, D.C., when Officer Branson shot Duckett, a Black man, in the head during a street fight over the arrest of his sister, Ellen Duckett. Duckett survived, was arrested three days later, pleaded guilty in Police Court and was fined $10 or thirty days. Washington's daily papers told the story as an attack on two policemen by a Black crowd.

episodes.title: Whipping of a Black barber in Washington, Georgia
episodes.summary: The whipping of a Black barber in Washington, Georgia, was an assault in which unnamed men took out a "negro barber" of the town, who had said he knew where Confederate gold was buried, and whipped him "nearly to death" to make him tell where it was. The Atlanta Constitution mentioned it in December 1881, in an article defending Jefferson Davis against a charge that he had misused Confederate funds.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Morgan Richards
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Morgan Richards took place near Gore, Hocking County, Ohio, on December 29, 1881, when a mob tried to take Richards, a farm hand accused of murdering his aunt, from the officers who had arrested him. The officers repulsed the mob and lodged him in the jail at Logan. Wire reports carried the story nationally as a crime item, and several predicted that he would still be lynched.

episodes.title: Driving out of Black strikebreakers at Coal Valley, West Virginia
episodes.summary: The driving out of Black strikebreakers at Coal Valley, West Virginia, took place in late 1881, when striking coal miners in Fayette County turned back the first group of Black miners that operators had brought from Virginia to replace them. Troops were then called to guard a second group, and the Wheeling Register printed two conflicting accounts of how serious the confrontation had been.

episodes.title: Lynching of Francis Jordan
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Francis Jordan was the reported killing of a Black woman at Las Vegas, New Mexico Territory, in late 1881, for the alleged murder of a Mrs. Feste. The only known account is a one-sentence item in a Kentucky weekly, which gave no date, no description of who killed her and no circumstances.

episodes.title: Killing of John Rhodes
episodes.summary: The killing of John Rhodes was the shooting of a Black man in his cabin on the Carson place, near Friars Point, Mississippi, by two masked men on a Saturday night in late 1881, probably December 3. Rhodes died of a shot to the head, and the only report supposed that the men had meant not to kill him but to frighten him off the place.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Searcy, Arkansas (1881)
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching at Searcy was an effort by a party of men in Searcy, Arkansas, in December 1881 to hang an unnamed Black man at the urging of a visitor who offered to show the town's young men how to "hang a nigger." Before the hanging could be carried out, the lynchers were attacked by a large number of persons, and the instigator fled. The only known account is a mocking item in the Searcy Record, reprinted in the Memphis Daily Appeal.

episodes.title: Fairfax County vigilance committee expulsion (1881)
episodes.summary: The Fairfax County vigilance committee expulsion was the forced departure of an unnamed Black man from part of Fairfax County, Virginia, in early December 1881, after a newly formed vigilance committee ordered him to leave for living with a white woman. He left almost at once, and the one newspaper report of it treated the episode as a joke.

episodes.title: Lynching of L. M. Bell
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of L. M. Bell was the hanging of a planter, called Colonel Bell, by a mob near Hamburg, Arkansas, close to the Louisiana line, on the night of December 27, 1881. Bell was accused of beating his wife so badly that she died at Christmas, and neighbors took him from his home and hanged him to a tree. Wire reports carried the story across the country, and several papers presented the lynching as deserved.

episodes.title: Shooting of Thomas Thompson
episodes.summary: The shooting of Thomas Thompson was the shooting of a Black man, described as "colored," by an officer named Griffith at Newark, Ohio, reported in December 1881. The only report found gave the officer's circumstance, that Thompson was "attempting to escape," and said nothing of whether he survived.

episodes.title: Beating of a hotel porter in Hinton, West Virginia (1881)
episodes.summary: The beating of a hotel porter in Hinton, West Virginia, was an assault on a Black porter by a man named Farris on the morning of 25 December 1881. Farris was arrested and brought before the mayor, but his friends' anger at the arresting officer led to an armed attack on the town's police the next night. Only the Richmond Dispatch's Hinton correspondent reported the beating; other papers carried only the attack on the police.

episodes.title: Hickory church burning
episodes.summary: The Hickory church burning was an attack in which a Black church at Hickory, Mississippi, was fired into and burned on a Monday night in late December 1881, and the town's calaboose was burned the same night. Three white men and a Black man were arrested on the charges, and a judge went to Hickory to investigate amid local alarm at the failure of officials to check lawlessness.

episodes.title: Hanging of three Mexican men on the Bandera road
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The hanging of three Mexican men on the Bandera road was the killing of three unnamed men whose bodies were found hanging from a tree northwest of San Antonio, Texas, on or shortly before 17 December 1881. The men were supposed to be robbers of travelers, and the papers said they had probably been lynched by German farmers of the neighborhood. Distant papers reported it only through a brief telegraphic item, and no one was identified.

episodes.title: Gold Park mining camp siege
episodes.summary: The Gold Park mining camp siege was a mob attack in late November or early December 1881 at the Gold Park mining camp near Leadville, Colorado, in which a crowd besieged a discharged blacksmith named Bayley (also printed Bagley), accused of killing the company foreman, and blew up his cabin with giant powder. Bayley was found dead in the ruins with a bullet wound through the heart, which the original dispatch attributed to suicide, although some later news briefs said the mob had blown him up. Carried on a single Leadville dispatch, the story ran in papers across the country as an example of Western lawlessness.

episodes.title: Killing of Patton and Mallory at Independence, Colorado
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The killing of Patton and Mallory took place at Independence, a mining camp about twenty miles west of Leadville, Colorado, shortly after dark on or about December 16, 1881, when townspeople chased down and shot two men described as desperadoes. The pair had been firing revolvers in the streets, and a crowd 'riddled' them with bullets, after which a vigilance committee formed to hang others of their kind, who fled. A single Leadville dispatch carried the story across the country, where papers headlined it as summary justice.

episodes.title: Burning of the Black schoolhouse at Empire, Kentucky
episodes.summary: The burning of the Black schoolhouse at Empire, Kentucky, was an arson in early June 1881 in which 'some unknown parties' set fire to a 'negro school house' at the coal-mining settlement of Empire. No one was reported hurt and no arrests were reported, but the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian called those responsible 'scoundrels' who were 'unfit to live' and urged that they be prosecuted.

episodes.title: Threats against Anderson Johnson (Bath County, Kentucky, 1881)
episodes.summary: The threats against Anderson Johnson followed his killing of his cousin Isaac Alfrey in Bath County, Kentucky, in early June 1881, and drove Johnson from his home under a warning of death. A widely reprinted wire brief said a mob had gone to hang him, but the Kentucky reports describe a court examination and an anonymous notice to leave rather than a mob. No report gives the race of either man.

episodes.title: Shooting of Will Wilkerson
episodes.summary: The shooting of Will Wilkerson took place at Malvern, Arkansas, on or about June 19, 1881, when a town marshal named Hall dangerously wounded Wilkerson, a Black man, while trying to arrest him. Wilkerson escaped to the woods and was still at large when the news was telegraphed from Little Rock the next day, with a number of people pursuing him.

episodes.title: Rose Hill attempted lynching (1881)
episodes.summary: The Rose Hill attempted lynching was an attempt by citizens in early June 1881 to lynch one of three white men accused of assaulting a blacksmith's daughter at Rose Hill, Lee County, apparently in Virginia. After capturing the man across the state line in Tennessee, his pursuers brought him back to the scene of the crime and prepared to lynch him; the only report does not say what followed.

episodes.title: Lynching of Juan Monterea
episodes.summary: The lynching of Juan Monterea was the hanging of a man accused of murder by a group of men in Taos County, New Mexico Territory, on the night of Saturday, June 11, 1881. Monterea had been arrested and jailed after Leon M. Gallagher, who had objected to his treatment of his mother, was killed with a hoe. According to a Santa Fe dispatch, a "large body of men" took him from jail and hanged him from the railing of the courthouse. The story ran as a short wire item in papers across the country in the following two weeks.

episodes.title: Lynching of Billy Leroy and Sam Potter
episodes.summary: The lynching of Billy Leroy and Sam Potter took place at Del Norte, Colorado, apparently on the night of May 22, 1881, when a party of men took the two captured stage robbers from the town jail and hanged them. Leroy, an escaped mail robber, and Potter had been brought to Del Norte as prisoners, and briefs printed across the country said they were lynched by citizens within an hour of arrival. A later account said a coroner's jury exonerated all concerned and that the dead men were brothers named Pond.

episodes.title: Lynching of Josh Shorter
episodes.summary: The lynching of Josh Shorter was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd near Eufaula, Alabama, on June 9, 1881. Shorter, accused of assaulting a young white girl the day before, was captured across the river in Georgia and hanged from a tree after a crowd kept him from the sheriff. The Savannah Morning News headlined the news "Speedy Vengeance," and a brief wire item carried it to papers as far away as Utah and California.

episodes.title: Reported torture of Abner Stanley and James Tibbetts
episodes.summary: The reported torture of Abner Stanley and James Tibbetts was a June 1881 episode in which, according to wire dispatches, fifteen to twenty armed men took four men from their homes in or near Sharp County, Arkansas, one Thursday night and tortured them in a glen to make them confess a robbery. Dispatches from Little Rock said Tibbetts and Stanley could not be found and were feared to have been tortured to death, while the other two men were jailed on suspicion of the robbery. Three weeks later the Sharp County Record denied that anything of the kind had happened in its part of the state.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jesse Myers and Frank Brown
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Jesse Myers and Frank Brown took place at New Madrid, Missouri, in late May 1881, when a mob organized to hang the two men, accused members of an outlaw gang, after they were brought to the town jail. Before the mob could act, Sheriff Walters and a few assistants removed the prisoners after dark and took them by river to St. Louis. The threat arose during a widely reported manhunt in southeast Missouri; Myers and Brown were later tried and hanged legally at New Madrid on July 15, 1881.

episodes.title: Beating of William Green by Shreveport police
episodes.summary: The beating of William Green by Shreveport police took place in Shreveport, Louisiana, in mid-June 1881, when Policeman Wimbish struck Green, a Black man wanted for larceny, several times over the head with his pistol during his arrest. A crowd of Black residents gathered and threatened to free Green, and the police chief ordered the arrest of its leaders. The only account is a Shreveport Times item, reprinted twice in a Baton Rouge paper, that tells the story from the officer's side.

episodes.title: Tracy City cabin shooting
episodes.summary: The Tracy City cabin shooting was an attack on June 11, 1881, in which unknown parties fired into the cabin of a Black man at Tracy City, Tennessee. No deaths or injuries were reported, and the case drew notice because Governor Hawkins offered a reward for the attackers.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Daniel McDonald
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Daniel McDonald took place at Ludington, Michigan, in early June 1881, when a crowd met him at the steamboat landing as officers brought him in on a charge of murdering a boy at a sawmill. The crowd called for him to be lynched, but no organized attempt was made and the sheriffs jailed him.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Utley and Henry Fisher
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of William Utley and Henry Fisher took place at Springfield, Tennessee, in late June 1881, after the two Black men were jailed on the night of June 27 on a charge of attempting to assault a white woman, Mrs. Mattie Davis. A Nashville dispatch predicted they would be lynched before morning, and a later brief said the people of Springfield had made preparations to lynch them. No report of the outcome was found.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of circus workers in Chesaning, Michigan
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of circus workers in Chesaning, Michigan, took place on June 8, 1881. A mob of about 300 townspeople tried to lynch four employees of a traveling circus who were held in connection with the killing of a village policeman. A posse of twelve men held the crowd back with revolvers and put the prisoners on a train to Saginaw City. Two of the four, Sim Robinson and William Murray, were described as "colored"; the case reached readers mainly through Chicago Tribune dispatches and Michigan state-news columns.

episodes.title: Killing of Jeff Hill
episodes.summary: The killing of Jeff Hill was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Constable J. M. Senac in Justice Langlois' court at New Iberia, Louisiana, on a Monday in June 1881, most likely June 6, while Hill was being tried on his wife's complaint that he had beaten her. Senac surrendered and was released on $500 bail, and a guard was placed at the jail after a rumor that Black residents meant to lynch him.

episodes.title: Lynching of Reimheimer
episodes.summary: The lynching of Reimheimer was the hanging of a German man, his name printed as Reimheimer and in several other spellings, by a band of about twenty to twenty-five unknown men who took him from the jail at Rockport, Atchison County, Missouri, early on June 11, 1881. He had been accused of shooting and robbing a man named Albert Angel near Irish Grove six days earlier, and he was awaiting trial when he was seized. A St. Joseph dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, often in news summaries beside the lynching of a Black man, John Taylor, in North Carolina the same weekend.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Purnell
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Henry Purnell took place near Tuckerman, Arkansas, on June 20, 1881, when a posse of citizens that had hunted him all day for an alleged rape captured him in the woods and nearly hanged him. Purnell, a farm hand of about sixty, was instead jailed, pleaded guilty before a justice the next morning, and was held under guard amid threats of lynching. The case reached papers from Memphis to Idaho through an Arkansas Gazette special and a shorter wire brief, none of which stated anyone's race.

episodes.title: Perry County Ku-Klux threats and Perryville newspaper fire
episodes.summary: The Perry County Ku-Klux threats and Perryville newspaper fire were a campaign of death threats, arson and armed intimidation at Perryville, Arkansas, in May and June 1881 against County Judge L. M. Harris, editor John L. Matthews and others by a group signing itself the "regular organized Ku-Klux." On a Sunday night, June 5 by the first dispatches, the newspaper office was set on fire; citizens put out the flames. Harris and Matthews fled before armed men came asking for them, and Governor Churchill sent General R. C. Newton to investigate. Matthews was shot dead outside his office in July in what dispatches called the same troubles.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Jim Myers from Newark Valley
episodes.summary: The expulsion of Jim Myers from Newark Valley was the forced departure, in late May or early June 1881, of Jim Myers (also spelled Meyers) and, by one account, a French partner from their cabin at Antelope Springs, Nevada, after stockmen ordered them out under threat of lynching. The men left without violence, and Nevada papers treated the episode as a brief item of local news.

episodes.title: Killing of J. E. Martin
episodes.summary: The killing of J. E. Martin was the murder of a merchant at Belknap, Texas, who was called from his house by three men on the night of June 9, 1881, led about half a mile away and shot dead. The men then robbed his store, and about two weeks later three men named McDonald were jailed at Graham for the crime amid fears that Belknap citizens would lynch them.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jesus Leon
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Jesus Leon was an effort in June 1881 at San Juan Capistrano, California, to lynch Leon, a man described as "a Mexican" who was accused of stabbing Enlogio Alvarez to death. Officers prevented the attempt and took Leon to jail in Los Angeles, where he was charged with murder the following month.

episodes.title: Shooting of Victor Davidson
episodes.summary: The shooting of Victor Davidson was a street shooting in Charlotte, North Carolina, on the night of Monday, June 20, 1881, in which one of three young white men fired at two Black men and wounded Davidson in the forehead. Davidson's condition was not known when the story appeared, and it was reported in his home town of Yorkville, South Carolina, because he had lived there.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Diddell
episodes.summary: The lynching of Charles Diddell was the hanging of a Black man by a mob from a bridge at Weston, Platte County, Missouri, on the evening of Sunday, June 12, 1881. Diddell, whose name was also printed "Didell," had been jailed that day, accused of raping and trying to kill a young white woman, and the mob took him from the jail and hanged him without trial. Papers from Chicago to Savannah carried the story; one wire brief named the victim "Ruse" and said his head was cut off after the hanging.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Bart Philips
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Bart Philips took place in Woodstock, Shenandoah County, Virginia, on the night of June 6, 1881, when a party of citizens formed to hang Philips, a Black man suspected of setting fire to the stables behind Welsh's Hotel. Philips was kept out of the crowd's reach, quietly arrested and committed to jail to await indictment.

episodes.title: Lynching of Robert Frye
episodes.summary: The lynching of Robert Frye was the hanging of a man described as a horse thief, whose body was found in the woods near Arlington, Texas, on a Tuesday evening in mid-June 1881. His killers left a placard reading "Horse thief" on the body and were not identified. The killing reached distant readers only as a one-sentence item in national news-brief columns.

episodes.title: Killing of Allen Chapman
episodes.summary: The killing of Allen Chapman was the shooting of a Black man by a band of masked, armed men at his cabin in Haywood district, Chattooga County, Georgia, on the night of about June 6, 1881. The band had come for a white girl who lived with him, and when Chapman met them with a shotgun they opened fire; he was reported dead. A Columbus dispatch carried in the Wheeling Intelligencer under the headline "Murder by Georgia Regulators" is the only known report.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jerry Hamilton
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jerry Hamilton was the fatal beating of a Black man by disguised men near Mount Vernon, Montgomery County, Georgia, on the night of May 2, 1881. Ten local men were charged under the federal civil rights bill and bound over to a United States grand jury; no report of a trial was found.

episodes.title: Killing of Dennis Brothen
episodes.summary: The killing of Dennis Brothen took place on the night of June 1, 1881, when a party of four young white men came to the home of Brothen, a Black man, in Camp County, Texas, near Jefferson, and two of them killed him. Brothen had fired on the party, killing Calvin Cope and mortally wounding Israel Hagrand, and the two unhurt men escaped. A brief dispatch from Jefferson carried the story to papers from West Virginia to California and Montana within a week.

episodes.title: Search for William Gauch
episodes.summary: The search for William Gauch was a manhunt by "citizens" of the county around Hillsboro, North Carolina, in late June 1881 for a Black man accused of raping a 10-year-old girl. The only report found, a Greensboro dispatch in the Chicago Daily Tribune, ended with the search under way and printed it under the headline "WRETCHES WHO SHOULD BE HUNG WHEN CAUGHT."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Albert Hayes
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Albert Hayes took place at about one o'clock in the morning of June 7, 1881, when a body of masked men broke into the county jail at Cairo, Illinois, to take and hang Hayes, a young Black prisoner. The men broke through a door and two of three cell locks but dispersed after the jail's keeper confronted them and fire bells were rung, and Hayes was held for trial.

episodes.title: Lynching of Cal Emory
episodes.summary: The lynching of Cal Emory took place about midnight on the night of June 13, 1881, when about twenty-five armed men forced the county jail at Dover, Pope County, Arkansas, shot Emory in his cell and hanged him on a gallows. Emory had been convicted of murdering a woman in Franklin County and sentenced to death, but Governor Churchill had commuted the sentence to twenty-one years in the penitentiary a few weeks earlier. It was the third attempt to lynch him, and Arkansas papers largely excused it as a rebuke to the governor's pardons.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Taylor
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Taylor took place before dawn on June 12, 1881, when a large party of men took Taylor, a young Black farm hand, from the Greensboro, North Carolina, jail and hanged him by a road about seven miles from Reidsville in Rockingham County. Taylor and George Gunn had been accused of assaulting the wife of Col. James Irwin on June 3, and an attempt to lynch them at the Wentworth jail on June 5 had failed. North Carolina papers largely endorsed the killing, and a Danville wire carried it nationally as a lynching done during an eclipse of the moon.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Taylor at Greensboro
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of John Taylor at Greensboro took place on the night of Monday, June 6, 1881, when, according to the Raleigh Observer, a large party of armed men rode into Greensboro, North Carolina, to take Taylor, a Black prisoner, from the Guilford County jail. Taylor was accused of raping a white woman, Mrs. James Irwin, near Reidsville in Rockingham County, and the sheriff removed him from the jail before the men could reach him. The attempt followed a raid on the Rockingham County jail at Wentworth, and five days later a larger party broke into the Greensboro jail, took Taylor out and hanged him.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Taylor
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Taylor took place on the night of June 11-12, 1881, when masked, mounted men broke into the Guilford County jail at Greensboro, North Carolina, and carried off Taylor, a Black farm hand accused of raping a white woman near Reidsville. They hanged him from a roadside oak in Rockingham County, and a coroner's jury found he had been hanged by unknown parties. A Danville wire report noting that the raid came during an eclipse of the moon ran across the country, while North Carolina papers mostly approved the lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of Estes Hairston and Lindsay
episodes.summary: The lynching of Estes Hairston and Lindsay was the hanging of two Black prisoners by about 150 masked men who took them from the jail at Danbury, Stokes County, North Carolina, on the night of Monday, June 20, 1881. Both had been held for months awaiting trial on charges of raping a white girl and a white woman. Wire reports said the hanging was generally approved, and a local correspondent published a defense of it.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Connors
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jim Connors took place at Espanola, New Mexico Territory, in June 1881, when masked men took Connors, accused with Harry Knowles of shooting a storekeeper in an attempted robbery, from his guards at night and hanged him from a telegraph pole. Knowles had already been shot dead by a citizens' party pursuing the pair. A wire report carried the episode across the country as the swift punishment of New Mexico "desperadoes", and no article in the coverage gives the race of either man.

episodes.title: Shooting of Allen and Alex Philips
episodes.summary: The shooting of Allen and Alex Philips took place on Sunday afternoon, 12 June 1881, when a deputy sheriff's party trying to arrest Allen Philips, a Black man, shot both brothers at Alex's house on Dr. Huguet's plantation below Baton Rouge, Louisiana. Both men were wounded, and a physician judged the wounds not fatal. The Baton Rouge Louisiana Capitolian reported the officers' version in full and declared them "fully justified," and the story reached other Louisiana papers as a one-line exchange item.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sidney King
episodes.summary: The lynching of Sidney King was the hanging of a Black man in Hernando County, Florida, after he was accused of shooting and cutting the three children of Sheriff J. B. Mickler on June 29, 1881. According to a Jacksonville dispatch, King was captured, confessed, and was hanged in the presence and with the approval of two hundred citizens. The dispatch ran in papers from Georgia to Wisconsin, and the Savannah Morning News, while condemning mob law, called the execution 'little wonder'.

episodes.title: Lynching of three Black men near Lockesburg, Arkansas
episodes.summary: The lynching of three Black men near Lockesburg, Arkansas, took place in early June 1881, when armed white men in Sevier County hunted down three unnamed men accused of robbing and murdering a farmer, R. F. Hall, and hanged them from trees at a ford on Rolling Fork Creek. The first man, called the ringleader, was hanged on his capture, and the other two were reported hanged on the night of Tuesday, June 7. Dispatches from Little Rock carried the story nationally within days, several presenting the hangings as deserved retribution.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of George Hadington
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of George Hadington took place at Savannah, Tennessee, in late June 1881, after Hadington, a Black man, was arrested on a charge of attempting to assault a fourteen-year-old white girl. The only report found, a brief in the Memphis Daily Appeal, said that the arrest caused "considerable excitement" and that threats to lynch him had been made, but it reported no attack.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jeff (Louisiana, 1881)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jeff was the hanging of a Black man in Louisiana in late June 1881, after he was accused of attacking the daughter of W. R. Turnage, his employer. The Farmerville Gazette's account, reprinted in three Louisiana papers, defended the killing as a case that did not admit of "law's delay."

episodes.title: Big Sandy railroad regulators, Carter County, Kentucky (1881)
episodes.doubt: race and deaths only in the Omaha Bee version; other wires say workmen, no race
episodes.summary: The Big Sandy railroad regulators were a gang in Carter County, Kentucky, led by the brothers David and William Patton, who in the summer of 1881 were reported to be driving workmen off the Big Sandy railroad. On 20 July 1881 the county judge asked Governor Blackburn for help, and the governor sent a general to the scene and offered rewards for the brothers' capture. One wire report described the workmen as "colored" and said several had been killed and others whipped, but the fuller dispatch carried by most papers named no race and no deaths.

episodes.title: Killing of the McKinney family on Kinney Creek
episodes.doubt: race unstated; date "last week" before Jun 1-9 reports, may be late May
episodes.summary: The killing of the McKinney family on Kinney Creek was an attack in late May 1881 in which regulators broke into a family's house on Kinney Creek in Carter County, Kentucky, and killed a man and two women named McKinney. It was reported as one of a series of regulator crimes in northeastern Kentucky, and one paper said the family was killed because they refused to be driven from the country. No report gives the victims' first names or race.

episodes.title: Franklin County moonshiners' attacks on Black residents (1881)
episodes.summary: The Franklin County moonshiners' attacks on Black residents were a series of whippings, robberies and expulsions carried out in late April 1881 by a disguised band led by the illicit distiller Dave Gillespie in the Running Bog neighborhood of Franklin County, Virginia. The band accused its victims of informing to federal revenue officers and ordered thirteen of them to leave the county on pain of death. Known only through the report of the revenue agent who had raided the district, the episode was carried nationally as a 'revival of Ku-Kluxism' and as evidence of local officials' indifference.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of the Boyces near Sturgeon
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of the Boyces near Sturgeon was a mob's attempt in May 1881 to lynch two young men named Boyce who had been arrested on the accusation of shooting a farmer's young son ten miles south of Sturgeon. The attempt failed, but the only report found predicted that a lynching would follow if the wounded boy died.

episodes.title: Lynching of Cherry Nichols
episodes.summary: The lynching of Cherry Nichols was the killing of a Black youth of about 17 or 18 who was taken from the Bienville Parish jail at Sparta, Louisiana, on a Saturday night in May 1881 by a party of forty to fifty armed men and later found hanged and shot. Nichols was being held for the grand jury, accused of raping and killing a young Black girl. Wire reports carried the story nationally, noting that the men were "mostly colored."

episodes.title: Killing of Alfred Wiggins
episodes.summary: The killing of Alfred Wiggins took place in Baltimore harbor early on May 12, 1881, when Policeman John B. Dorsey shot Wiggins, a Black man he suspected of stealing grain from the schooner Ida, and Wiggins fell overboard and drowned. A coroner's jury found the same day that Dorsey, on duty and in danger of his life, had been justified in using his pistol. Wire services carried it as a short crime item headed "A Dead Thief," and weekly digests repeated it the next week.

episodes.title: Killing of Jerry Hamilton
episodes.summary: The killing of Jerry Hamilton was the fatal beating of a Black plantation worker by masked men near Red Bluff, Montgomery County, Georgia, on the night of May 2, 1881. A mass meeting at Mount Vernon denounced it, and in June ten local men were brought to Savannah on a federal civil rights warrant.

episodes.title: Grand Haven jail lynching attempt (1881)
episodes.summary: The Grand Haven jail lynching attempt was a march by several hundred farmers on the Ottawa County jail at Grand Haven, Michigan, on the night of May 14, 1881, to take out and hang Albertus Voskamp, a hired man accused of murdering his employer. Militia ordered out by the governor met the crowd at the jail, and after a parley it went home without violence, warning that it would return if Voskamp were not convicted. Voskamp, described as a Prussian or German, was later convicted and sentenced to life.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of J. H. Floyd
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of J. H. Floyd took place in Arizona Territory in May 1881, when armed men from Florence pursued Sheriff J. P. Gabriel and his prisoner to Casa Grande and demanded Floyd at gunpoint. Floyd had been arrested for shooting dead an elderly Florence resident, Charles Bernard, known as "American Charley." The sheriff held off the party until a train arrived and lodged Floyd in the Tucson jail; Floyd was later convicted of manslaughter, a verdict Arizona papers denounced so sharply that one regretted the lynching had failed.

episodes.title: Lynching at the Talladega picnic (1881)
episodes.summary: The lynching at the Talladega picnic was the hanging of an unnamed Black man near Talladega, Alabama, in May 1881, by the father and fellow members of a picnic party who accused him of choking the father's young daughter to death and robbing her. He was hanged to a tree near the falls of a river and his body was left hanging. The story ran across the country as a wire item, often under headlines that approved of the killing, such as 'Justifiable Lynching'.

episodes.title: Lynching of Pat Rhodes
episodes.summary: The lynching of Pat Rhodes was the hanging of a wounded prisoner near Bayne's store, between New Madrid and Sikeston, Missouri, on the morning of May 12, 1881. Rhodes was one of four men accused of shooting into William Knox's house and killing a member of the posse sent after them. The wire said vigilantes hanged him, while local letters said only that he was found hanging in a stable while under guard.

episodes.title: Killing of James Hamilton at Mill Springs
episodes.summary: The killing of James Hamilton at Mill Springs was the shooting of Hamilton and the wounding and capture of Jesse Myers by a search party under Capt. W. T. Leeper near Mill Springs, Wayne County, Missouri, at daybreak on May 21, 1881. The men were wanted for shooting the county's sheriff and collector the day before; a third, Frank Brown, surrendered that evening. Threats to lynch Myers and Brown led the New Madrid County sheriff to remove them to St. Louis, and both were later convicted and hanged.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Patton (Potter)
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Patton (also reported as John Potter) was the killing of a prisoner charged with horse stealing, who was taken from a deputy sheriff on the road near Kerrville, Texas, in May 1881 and shot dead. No one was identified, and the case reached papers outside Texas as an example of Texas "lawlessness".

episodes.title: Lynching of Matt Butts
episodes.summary: The lynching of Matt Butts was the hanging of a Black man by a mob near Arlington, Early County, Georgia, on or about May 31, 1881. Butts had been accused of stabbing Maj. W. J. Bethea to death, and after his capture he was taken by a mob, reported as 200 men, and hanged to a tree. An Atlanta wire carried the news to papers in the Midwest and West, while a Georgia paper passed on a local account that called him Matt Horton.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching on Union Street, Bellaire (1881)
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching on Union Street, Bellaire, was an incident late on the evening of Monday, May 30, 1881, in which a crowd of men from Wheeling was reported to be preparing to lynch a Bellaire, Ohio, resident on Union street. Help arrived before the crowd acted, and the only report said no serious damage was done. The episode is known from a single line in the Wheeling Register's Bellaire column, which named no one and gave neither a cause nor the man's race.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Pete Megley
episodes.doubt: printed and retracted in the same issue (false report)
episodes.summary: The reported lynching of Pete Megley was a hanging that Nevada papers said had taken place in the cattle valleys of White Pine County in about May 1881, when Megley and another man were rumored to have been found hanging from a tree. Reports blamed ranchmen who suspected the men of cattle stealing, but the story was retracted, revived and denied over several weeks, and no body, inquest or arrest was reported. No report gives the race of either man.

episodes.title: Presidents Island workhouse beatings
episodes.summary: The Presidents Island workhouse beatings were assaults on prisoners at the county workhouse on Presidents Island, near Memphis, Tennessee, described by Black prisoners to a county court committee that visited on 28 March 1881. Prisoners said Deputy Sheriff Collins and two guards had struck them with an iron poker, a pistol and sticks and whipped them with a barrel stave. The Memphis papers headlined the report for the filth it found, and the committee later said it was satisfied that no cruel treatment was practiced.

episodes.title: Killing of Ben Burnett
episodes.summary: The killing of Ben Burnett was the fatal shooting of a Black man by the city marshal of Lamonte, Missouri, ten miles west of Sedalia, on the evening of March 1, 1881. The marshal, named in the fullest account as Philip Zilhart, said Burnett had refused arrest after attacking a woman and advanced on him with a club, and a coroner's jury found the shooting justified. Wire reports carried the story to Memphis and Chicago, and a longer Sedalia dispatch ran in the Dallas Herald under the headline "A Brutal Negro Done For."

episodes.title: Lynching of Sam Gaines
episodes.summary: The lynching of Sam Gaines was the killing of a Black man by a party of masked men at his cabin ten miles north of Springfield, Robertson County, Tennessee, near the Kentucky line, on the night of March 1, 1881. Gaines was called from his bed and shot to death in front of his wife and children, and no one was reported arrested. Tennessee papers presented the killing as the latest in a run of mob violence in Robertson County, while Kentucky papers repeated a charge that he had been banished for arson.

episodes.title: Attack on the funeral of A. Oscar Jones
episodes.summary: The attack on the funeral of A. Oscar Jones was a street assault in Philadelphia in late February or early March 1881, in which boys stoned Black mourners in the funeral procession of the captain of the Grey Invincibles, a Black militia company. A running fight with stones and pistol shots followed until police quelled the crowd; no serious injuries were reported.

episodes.title: Whipping of Dorritt Banks
episodes.summary: The whipping of Dorritt Banks was the public thrashing of a Black youth by a white man in the upper part of Greenville County, South Carolina, in early March 1881. Accused of forcibly kissing a white schoolgirl, Banks was whipped by her father before witnesses after Banks's father chose the thrashing over a prosecution. A Greenville dispatch printed in the Chicago Daily Tribune presented the case as an example of a "novel" and "economical" way of punishing crime.

episodes.title: Hunnewell Furnace Regulators attack
episodes.summary: The Hunnewell Furnace Regulators attack was a night fight on March 20, 1881, at Brown-town, Greenup County, Kentucky, between a band of "Regulators" and Black ore-diggers whose hiring it opposed. One Black digger was wounded in the face and one Regulator was shot, the furnace was put under armed guard, and eight of the band were jailed. Papers carried it as part of a Regulator "reign of terror" around Grayson and in adjoining Greenup County.

episodes.title: Lynching of Wesley Harrison Smith
episodes.summary: The lynching of Wesley Harrison Smith was the shooting of a Black man near Campbellsburg, Henry County, Kentucky, on the night of Monday, March 7, 1881, by masked "vigilantes" hidden in a barn he was accused of setting on fire. A Cincinnati detective had led him into the trap, and Smith was shot fleeing arrest; he died hours later in a blacksmith shop. The wire version stressed the report that some of the masked men sat on the coroner's jury.

episodes.title: Manhunt for the assailant of Jane Cunningham
episodes.summary: The manhunt for the assailant of Jane Cunningham was a search in March and April 1881 for an unnamed Black man accused of assaulting a young white woman near Orangeburg, South Carolina, and escaping into a swamp. A News and Courier dispatch printed under the headline "A Negro Wants Lynching" said he was being "hotly pursued" and "may have a short shift" if found. Two Black men were arrested as suspects elsewhere; the Newberry Herald wrote that the first, reportedly forced to confess by threats with "the pistol and the rope," would probably have been lynched at Orangeburg.

episodes.title: Lynching of Green Harris, Giles Peck, John Woods and Burt Hoskins
episodes.summary: The lynching of Green Harris, Giles Peck, John Woods and Burt Hoskins took place at about midnight in early March 1881 near New Haven Church, seven miles north of Jonesboro in Craighead County, Arkansas, when a band of masked men took the four Black prisoners from their guards and hanged them. The men had been accused of the murder of Mattie Ishmael, a planter's daughter, and committed to await the grand jury. Wire dispatches from Little Rock carried the story to papers across the country, most of which reported it as a just retribution.

episodes.title: Lynching of Tom Gordon
episodes.summary: The lynching of Tom Gordon was the hanging of a man accused of killing the city marshal of Socorro, New Mexico Territory, by a mob at Socorro in March 1881. Gordon had escaped to Albuquerque, was rearrested there and taken back to Socorro, where a mob numbered in the hundreds hanged him to a water tank. The story reached eastern and southern papers through a single Kansas City dispatch, reprinted widely in mid-March.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ed Turner
episodes.summary: The lynching of Ed Turner took place on the night of Saturday, March 12, 1881, at Mississippi City in Harrison County, Mississippi, when a party of fifty or sixty armed and masked men took Turner, a Black man, from the town jail and hanged him to a tree. Turner was being held on an accusation that he had raped a white woman, Mrs. Mike McIntosh. Mississippi and Tennessee papers reported local approval of the killing, and a short telegraphic account ran from California to New Hampshire.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Dieckman
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of William Dieckman took place at Hilltown, St. Louis County, Missouri, on March 17, 1881, when 75 to 100 farmers gathered intending to lynch Dieckman, who was jailed for the fatal stabbing of his employer, Henry W. Mertz. No attack on the prisoner was reported, and in July he was convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to 18 years. Papers from Wheeling to Dallas carried the story, one under the headline "Threatened Lynching."

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Varner
episodes.doubt: thin: only one wire copy says lynched; others end with the capture
episodes.summary: The lynching of Frank Varner was the reported hanging and shooting of a Black man taken from the jail at Fort Worth, Texas, in March 1881, a few hours after he was jailed on a charge of assaulting a young woman. The story reached newspapers across the country through a single St. Louis Republican special, and only one copy of it, in the Cheyenne Daily Leader, reported the lynching; every other copy ended with the prediction that Varner "will probably be lynched."

episodes.title: Charleston, Illinois, vigilance committee whippings and expulsions (1881)
episodes.summary: The Charleston, Illinois, vigilance committee whippings and expulsions took place in March 1881, when masked vigilantes at Charleston, in Coles County, hung and whipped three men accused of belonging to a gang of thieves and house-burners and then ordered some twenty other people out of town. No one was reported killed, and nearly all of those warned left within a day. The story ran in papers across the country, and several editors cited it as evidence that lynching was not confined to the South.

episodes.title: Lynching of an unknown man near Jacksboro, Texas (1881)
episodes.summary: The lynching of an unknown man near Jacksboro, Texas, came to light on March 19, 1881, when his body was found hanging by the neck with nine bullet holes in Howard Valley, nine miles from the town. He was said to be a horse thief, and his killers were not identified. A single Jacksboro dispatch carried the case to newspapers from Virginia to Nevada, two of which headed it "LYNCHED."

episodes.title: Regulator attack on Black ore-diggers at Hunnewell Furnace
episodes.summary: The Regulator attack on Black ore-diggers at Hunnewell Furnace was a night clash on March 20, 1881, at Browntown, Greenup County, Kentucky, between about twelve or fifteen Regulators and a party of Black workers hired by the furnace. One Black man was wounded in the face and one Regulator was shot, and eight of the band were later reported jailed at Catlettsburg. A Grayson dispatch presented the clash as part of a Regulator "reign of terror" around Grayson and in adjoining Greenup County.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Joe Ebright
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Joe Ebright took place at Las Vegas, New Mexico, in March 1881, after Ebright, a saloon keeper, shot and killed James H. Curry, a freight conductor on the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe railroad, and railroad men talked of hanging him. The sheriff swore in special deputies and fortified the jail, and a justice of the peace discharged Ebright three days later when no one appeared to prosecute. It drew national notice because a Philadelphia dispatch misidentified the dead man as James Currie, the killer of the actor Benjamin Porter.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Parrott (Big Nose George)
episodes.summary: The lynching of George Parrott, known as "Big Nose George," took place in Rawlins, Wyoming Territory, on the night of March 22, 1881, when a party of men took the condemned prisoner from the county jail and hanged him from a telegraph pole. Parrott had been sentenced to death for the killing of two deputy sheriffs and had tried to break jail earlier that evening. The story ran in papers from California to Rhode Island, which dwelt on the escape attempt, the failed first hanging and his last words.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jack Roberts
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jack Roberts was the hanging in March 1881 of a man accused of shooting Thomas A. Greatorex at Durango, Colorado, carried out by what dispatches called a band of vigilantes. The first reports put the lynching at Durango on the night of March 25; a later St. Louis dispatch said vigilantes took him from two men who had captured him for a reward and hanged him to a tree. Newspapers across the country ran the story as a brief item, several describing Roberts as one of a band of "noted desperadoes"; none gave his race.

episodes.title: Lynching of Felix (Gus) Barnes
episodes.summary: The lynching of Felix Barnes, also reported as Gus Barnes, was the killing of a young Black man by a party of citizens near Sparta, Georgia, in late March 1881. Accused of attacking a young white woman named as Miss Lizzie Johnson, he was pursued, caught, hanged and shot. Dispatches from Sparta, Atlanta and Macon carried the story across the country, and the Atlanta version reported that the killing was approved locally and that 'nothing will be done'.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dick Osborne
episodes.summary: The lynching of Dick Osborne took place at Ainsworth, Washington Territory, on the night of March 26-27, 1881, when a party of masked men took Osborne from the officers holding him and hanged him. Osborne, known as "Black Dick," had been arrested that day for stabbing a gambler named Alonzo Babb, who later died of his wounds. Regional papers reported that the hanging met with public approval, and a short wire carried the story to papers across the country.

episodes.title: Roping and banishment of a Hayesville man at Loudonville, Ohio
episodes.summary: The roping and banishment of a Hayesville man at Loudonville, Ohio, took place on Saturday, March 26, 1881, when a group of townspeople took an unnamed man from the town marshal, put a rope around his neck and drove him from town. He was released after swearing never to return, and no paper stated his race. A Cleveland dispatch about the affair ran in papers across the country under approving headlines such as "Served Him Right."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of the Poe brothers at Winchester, Tennessee (March 1881)
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of the Poe brothers at Winchester, Tennessee, took place at the end of March 1881, when about forty masked men set out at night for the jail holding John and Cicero Poe, who were accused of murder. Two townsmen met the party a mile from town and persuaded it to turn back, and no one was hurt. Wire reports on the brothers' conviction weeks later still recalled the "threatened lynching" that had "created so much excitement at Winchester."

episodes.title: Goose Creek masked raid on William Jones
episodes.summary: The Goose Creek masked raid on William Jones was a night attack by a band of disguised men on a Black blacksmith and a woman in the Goose Creek neighborhood of Bedford County, Virginia, shortly before March 5, 1881. The attackers whipped Jones and inflicted a severe injury on the woman, whose race the reports gave differently. Virginia and national papers called it a 'terrible and nameless' or 'inhuman' outrage, and one dispatch insisted it was without parallel in the state.

episodes.title: Killing of Stephen Wade
