episodes.summary: The killing of Stephen Wade was the night shooting of a sixty-year-old Black man at his home in a Black settlement near Palestine, Darke County, Ohio, by a band of twenty to thirty masked horsemen in October 1878. Wade and his family had been accused of thefts and ordered by red-ink notices to leave the county. Newspapers headlined it as "Ohio Ku-Klux", and men indicted for it were arrested in Indiana and Ohio and one was tried for murder in March 1879.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of J. N. Jones
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of J. N. Jones was an incident at Benton, Montana Territory, reported in March 1881, in which Jones, a man from Meagher county, narrowly escaped being lynched. He was spared on account of his family and on a promise to leave town within three days, and was said to have left the country afterward.

episodes.title: Lynching of Winn at Ivanpah
episodes.summary: The lynching of Winn at Ivanpah was the hanging of an Indian man by four masked men at the mining camp of Ivanpah, San Bernardino County, California, in March 1881. Winn was accused of shooting dead Daniel Keistler, or Kestler, a stock-raiser, and other Indians had caught him and handed him over before the masked men took him out at night. A San Francisco wire carried the story across the country, often under headlines that made a joke of the victim being an Indian.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of an Indian prisoner at Fort Colville
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of an Indian prisoner at Fort Colville took place in Washington Territory in mid-March 1881, when citizens marched to take from jail an Indian accused of shooting a man known as Dutch Joe. The military took charge of the prisoner and locked him in the Fort Colville guardhouse, and he was not harmed. The episode reached readers through a Walla Walla wire item, a territorial weekly, and a Pennsylvania paper printing letters from a cavalry officer at the fort.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Fritz W. Haas and Catherine Hoffart
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Fritz W. Haas and Catherine Hoffart was a threat by a crowd at Union, Franklin County, Missouri, in late February or early March 1881 against two prisoners held in the county jail on a murder indictment. Officers removed the pair by night to St. Louis, and no one was hurt. The episode is known only from a single wire paragraph carried by several papers in Tennessee, Mississippi, Arkansas, Missouri and Indiana.

episodes.title: Burning of the colored school at Fair Haven, New Jersey
episodes.doubt: the only attribution of the arson names Black residents
episodes.summary: The burning of the colored school at Fair Haven, New Jersey, was the destruction by fire of the school house for Black children in Fair Haven, Monmouth County, late on a Wednesday night in February 1881, during a dispute over admitting Black children to the town's new white school. An Associated Press dispatch attributed the fire to Black residents and named a Black suspect, but no arrest was reported. The fire sharpened Fair Haven's "school war," which led to the white school's closing and a state law against excluding children by color.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Merrill
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Charles Merrill took place on February 27, 1881, in China, Kennebec County, Maine, when a crowd of local people threatened Merrill, a young man held by a deputy sheriff on the charge of murdering his mother. Officers took him to the jail at Augusta that day for fear of an attempt to lynch him after dark, and he was later convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment. Papers treated the killing itself as the most atrocious murder in the state's history and mentioned the threat as a side detail.

episodes.title: Lynching of an unnamed Black man in Bosque County, Texas (1881)
episodes.summary: The lynching of an unnamed Black man in Bosque County, Texas, was reported in March 1881 as the hanging by a mob of a man accused of raping a white woman. The only account found is one sentence in a column of state news in the San Marcos Free Press, which gives no name, date, or details of the killing.

episodes.title: Expulsion of a labor agent near Pulaski, Tennessee (1881)
episodes.summary: The expulsion of a labor agent near Pulaski, Tennessee, took place in early 1881, when a mob drove away a man who had recruited about forty Black laborers to move to Jackson County, Arkansas. The laborers reached Jackson County, and the mob was described as opposed to "the negroes leaving that section." The episode is known from a single brief in an Arkansas newspaper.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Henry Hill
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Henry Hill took place at Hartwell, Hart County, Georgia, in early March 1881, when a crowd of about three hundred people gathered around the jail threatening to lynch Hill, a Black prisoner recaptured after the killing of the county jailer. No attack on the jail was reported, and Hill was later tried, convicted and hanged under a court sentence before a crowd of several thousand.

episodes.title: Whipping of the Bellamy family by Kentucky regulators
episodes.summary: The whipping of the Bellamy family was a night attack in Kentucky in March 1881, in which a masked party of self-styled regulators whipped a man named Bellamy, his three sons and two neighborhood women "for alleged immorality." The raiders also threatened to hang Bellamy's son-in-law, John Snider, who escaped and went into hiding. Papers reported it as part of a regulator "reign of terror" around Grayson.

episodes.title: Lynching at Refugio, Texas (1881)
episodes.summary: The lynching at Refugio, Texas, was the killing of an unnamed Black man by a mob in late February or early March 1881, after he was accused of raping a white woman. He was taken from the jail and, according to the Memphis Appeal, hanged. The case survives only as a short exchange paragraph reprinted in Tennessee and Texas papers, one of which called his death "deserved."

episodes.title: Reported slave sale at Fairview, West Virginia
episodes.doubt: thin: one telegram, doubted by the first paper to print it
episodes.summary: The reported slave sale at Fairview, West Virginia, was an auction of Black men and women described as "the regular annual sale of slaves," said to have been held in front of the Fairview court house on a Saturday in late March 1881. The claim rested on a single special telegram relayed through Pittsburgh and reprinted in a few Northern papers. The first paper to print it suggested the correspondent had mistaken the contracting of convict labor for a slave sale.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Doc Wilson
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Doc Wilson took place in March 1881, when a mob reportedly organized in Macon, Georgia, to lynch Wilson, a young Black barber accused of killing a young Macon man, James Tinley. Officers who had brought Wilson back from Florida lodged him in the Atlanta jail instead, and no attack on him was reported. He was tried for murder in Macon in December 1881, in a case a correspondent said had stirred more feeling than any other before the court.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Henry Hunt
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Henry Hunt took place in January 1881, when crowds at Santa Ana and Los Angeles, California, threatened to hang Hunt, a prisoner charged with the fatal shooting of George W. Gillis at El Monte. Officers kept Hunt in custody, and he was later convicted and sentenced to life in prison. The episode reached papers across the country through an anecdote in which a speaker broke up the mob by proposing a collection for the dead officer's widow and orphans.

episodes.title: Lynching of Rupe at Tomlinson, Arkansas
episodes.summary: The lynching of Rupe was the killing by a mob of a man named Rupe at Tomlinson, Arkansas, after he shot a man named Fuller, an event reported in early March 1881. It is known only from a one-sentence news brief, which said the townspeople found the shooting "despicable" and that "A mob murdered the murderer." The same paragraph circulated as filler in Pennsylvania, Illinois and Ohio papers between March and April 1881.

episodes.title: Hanging of three horse thieves in Hill County, Texas
episodes.summary: The hanging of three horse thieves in Hill County, Texas, was the reported killing, shortly before April 8, 1881, of three unnamed men accused of horse theft by "vigilantes of Johnson county" who overtook them in neighboring Hill County. The story circulated only as a one-line wire item, and no report named the men, gave their race, or described the hanging.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ofrio Baca
episodes.summary: The lynching of Ofrio Baca was the hanging of a prisoner accused of murdering A. M. Conklin, editor of the Socorro Sun, by vigilantes at Socorro, New Mexico Territory, at the end of March 1881. Brought to Socorro under arrest from Mexico, he was taken from the jail and hanged from the gate of the courthouse yard. The territorial press reported the killing as Conklin's murder "revenged," and its gallows headline became a joke in eastern papers.

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Seagraves
episodes.summary: The killing of Henry Seagraves was the shooting of a deputy United States marshal and revenue officer by a party of unidentified men in Macon County, Tennessee, on the night of April 8, 1881. The attackers robbed his body and escaped, and the collector of internal revenue at Nashville attributed the killing to Seagraves's part in breaking up illicit distilleries. The story ran as a wire item in daily papers from Washington to Savannah and as a one-line brief in rural weeklies.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Joseph Warsaw
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Joseph Warsaw took place in Warsaw, Illinois, in mid-March 1881, when citizens of the town threatened to lynch a man accused of assaulting a young woman. The authorities removed him to Carthage for safety, and no attack on him was reported. The episode is known from a single brief in the Cairo Bulletin, which did not state the man's race.

episodes.title: Lynching of Reddy McDonald
episodes.summary: The lynching of Reddy McDonald was the hanging of a jailed man by vigilantes at Sidney, Nebraska, in the early hours of Sunday, April 3, 1881. About thirty men took him from his cell and hanged him from a tree in the court-house yard; a coroner's jury found him killed by persons unknown. A Cheyenne Daily Leader dispatch calling him "a noted cut-throat" ran in papers across the country.

episodes.title: Lynching of Francisco Jimeno
episodes.summary: The lynching of Francisco Jimeno was the hanging of a young sheepherder by about one hundred citizens near Lompoc, at Santa Rita in Santa Barbara County, California, in early April 1881. Jimeno, described as Mexican or Indian, was held on suspicion of the rape and murder of Mrs. Louisa Sargent and was taken after the inquest and hanged to a tree near the scene. The local press applauded the hanging, while some eastern papers soon reported that the wrong man had been lynched.

episodes.title: Lynching of Judy Metts
episodes.summary: The lynching of Judy Metts took place on the night of April 9, 1881, when disguised horsemen took Metts, a Black woman accused of burning a barn, from a constable near Martin's Depot in Laurens County, South Carolina, and hanged her from a tree. A coroner's jury blamed persons unknown, and Governor Hagood offered $200 for each lyncher, but no arrests were reported. Because the victim was a woman accused of a property crime, several South Carolina papers called the killing murder and debated lynching for months.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Hayes White
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Hayes White took place on April 29, 1881, when a large crowd boarded a train at Forrest City, Arkansas, to lynch White, a Black prisoner accused of killing Sheriff W. F. Beattie of Crittenden County. The conductor had hidden White in the baggage car, and the crowd left without him. White was tried at Marion and hanged there on June 10 before a crowd reported at 2,000, most of them Black.

episodes.title: McLauren family killings, Edwards County, Texas
episodes.summary: The McLauren family killings took place on the afternoon of Tuesday, April 19, 1881, when a party of about fifteen armed men rode to the house of a man named McLauren on the Frio in Edwards County, Texas, and killed McLauren, his wife and a young man named Lease who lived with them. No motive, accusation or suspect for the killings was reported, and nothing in the house was taken. Papers across the country carried the story as a 'mysterious triple murder'.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Mormon
episodes.summary: The lynching of Charles Mormon was the hanging of a Leadville stage driver by vigilantes at Durango, Colorado, in April 1881, after he was accused of shooting and killing Polk Prindle in a theater and gambling house. Vigilantes took him from the jail late at night and hanged him to a tree before a crowd of citizens, warning that anyone who cut him down before morning would be killed. A Denver Republican dispatch from Durango carried the story to papers across the country within days, and reprints spelled his surname at least five different ways.

episodes.title: Killing of Posey Drew
episodes.summary: The killing of Posey Drew was the fatal stabbing of Drew, a Black dance-house keeper, at the door of his house on Cary Street in Richmond, Virginia, on the night of April 16, 1881, by a member of a party of white youths from Manchester. A coroner's jury found that John Bowen struck the blow with his brother Charles as accessory, and a Hustings Court jury convicted John Bowen and sentenced him to three years in the penitentiary, while Charles was acquitted. Most of the coverage came from the Richmond Daily Dispatch, while a wire report printed elsewhere called the attackers unknown.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Devine
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jim Devine was the hanging of a man known as Jim Devine, alias Jones, by a party of men at Raton City, New Mexico Territory, in mid-April 1881, after he was accused of assaulting two men there. Telegraph reports from Denver placed the lynching "near Las Vegas" on Saturday night, April 16, and described Devine as an escaped California convict with a reward on his head. The story ran as a brief in papers from California to Kentucky, usually beside other Western killings.

episodes.title: Lynching of Lunn Whittaker
episodes.summary: The lynching of Lunn Whittaker was the hanging of a Black prisoner by twenty to thirty masked, armed men who took him from the county jail at Quincy, Gadsden County, Florida, early on Sunday, April 17, 1881. Whittaker, described as one of the men implicated in the murder of James McJunkin, was hanged from an oak in the woods just east of town while the jail guards were made to watch. Wire briefs carried the story to papers in several states through late April, often garbling his name and the place.

episodes.title: 1881 Louisville freight platform strike
episodes.summary: The 1881 Louisville freight platform strike was a wage strike by platform hands at the Louisville & Nashville Railroad freight depot in Louisville, Kentucky, in April 1881, during which the strikers ordered that the "colored laborers" hired in their places be told they would not be allowed to work. No violence was reported, and the strike ended within four days after other roads raised wages and the L&N found enough replacement men.

episodes.title: Killing of Kiah Baker
episodes.summary: The killing of Kiah Baker was the fatal shooting of an elderly Black man on a road about three miles northeast of Hopkinsville, Christian County, Kentucky, in mid-April 1881. Before he died, Baker said one of three passing horsemen had shot him, while a rival story held that he was shot robbing a hen roost. A young man, Jas. B. Cannon, was arrested after boasting that he had done it, but was acquitted, and the local paper later recorded the killing as an assassination by "unknown parties."

episodes.title: Lynching of John Winn
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Winn took place around midnight of April 27-28, 1881, when a masked mob of thirty to forty men entered the jail at Paris, Kentucky, and shot Winn dead in his cell. Winn was being held under indictment for the murder of William Moreland, a young man of Bourbon County. A coroner's jury found that he had been killed by persons unknown, and the story ran in papers from Washington to Kansas.

episodes.title: Near-lynching of Billy Reed
episodes.summary: The near-lynching of Billy Reed took place at O'Neill City, Holt County, Nebraska, in late March or early April 1881, when residents nearly lynched a cowboy held for the fatal shooting of Sheriff Barney Kearns. No one was killed; the prisoner was moved to the jail at West Point, and the local paper credited the dying sheriff's plea for forgiveness with saving him. Reed was acquitted of the murder that October, and none of the reports gave the race of anyone involved.

episodes.title: Mock trial and hanging at Anderson's Bridge
episodes.summary: The mock trial and hanging at Anderson's Bridge took place on Saturday, about April 23, 1881, when a crowd of white men at Anderson Bridge on Lynch's Creek, near Williamsburg, South Carolina, put a Black man suspected of housebreaking through a mock trial and briefly hanged him to force a confession. He was cut down alive and later had three of the party arrested. The story, first told by the Williamsburg Herald as an affair done 'more for amusement than anything else,' ran in South Carolina papers and as a wire item in Washington and Maine.

episodes.title: Pascagoula railroad platform assault
episodes.summary: The Pascagoula railroad platform assault was a fight on the morning of Monday, April 4, 1881, on the railroad platform at Pascagoula, Mississippi, in which five white young men from Mobile set upon a young Black man after the two sides had cursed each other. A local magistrate broke up the fight, and no one was arrested. A Memphis roundup of regional news later reduced the episode to a report that the Mobile men had "whipped a negro."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Frank Ray and Maxwell Smith
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Frank Ray and Maxwell Smith took place near Sherman, Texas, in the spring of 1881, when the two men were arrested on charges of attempting outrages on little girls and local citizens grew so excited that the prisoners had to be removed to keep them from being lynched. No attack followed, and both men were later dealt with in the Sherman courts, Smith with a $25 fine and Ray with a five-year prison term. None of the reports gives the race of the accused men or of the girls.

episodes.title: Killing of Charles Dew
episodes.summary: The killing of Charles Dew was the death of a Black farmer in Riley Township, Clinton County, Michigan, who was found hanging in his granary with his head laid open in late August 1881, months after masked men had tarred and feathered him. Early dispatches tied his death to his attempt to prosecute the tarring party, and several papers called it a lynching. One member of the tarring party later confessed and named seven others, but the only murder trial, of Dew's wife and her brother Ben Cooper, ended in acquittal in 1882.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Taylor at Chattanooga
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of John Taylor took place at Chattanooga, Tennessee, on the evening of April 6, 1881, when a large crowd met Taylor, a prisoner accused of murder, on his arrival by train amid talk of lynching him. Officers lodged him in jail without harm. The crowd drew one sentence at the end of a Knoxville report on his capture, which the papers treated as the news.

episodes.title: Lynching of James Fowler
episodes.summary: The lynching of James Fowler took place at Custer City, Dakota Territory, early on February 7, 1881, when about twenty masked men took Fowler, known as "Fly Specked Billy," from Sheriff John T. Code and his deputies and hanged him from a pine tree. Fowler had been arrested a few hours earlier, accused of shooting dead Abe Barnes, a freighter, in a Custer City billiard hall. A Deadwood dispatch carried the story across the West and Midwest, and the local Custer Chronicle printed an approving account with testimony from both inquests.

episodes.title: Lynching of a gambler at Baldwin, Florida
episodes.summary: The lynching of a gambler at Baldwin, Florida, was a killing at some point before March 1881 that the Tallahassee Economist described as 'a visitation from Judge Lynch' upon the gamblers who worked from the town. It is known only from a passing reference in a Florida editorial on railroad swindlers, which gives no date, name or race for the man killed.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joseph Snyder
episodes.summary: The lynching of Joseph Snyder took place on December 27, 1880, when a crowd seized Snyder from a detective at Santee's Mills, near Bethlehem in Northampton County, Pennsylvania, and hanged him from a chestnut tree. Snyder, a boarder accused of killing Jacob and Annie Gogle with an axe hours earlier, was hanged while the coroner's jury sat upstairs in the victims' house. Newspapers called it the first lynching in Pennsylvania, and no one was indicted after a judge told the county grand jury the killing was murder.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Bruce's accused killer
episodes.summary: The lynching of Frank Bruce's accused killer was the killing by a mob, in Tensas Parish, Louisiana, in early 1881, of an unnamed Black man arrested for the murder of a store clerk. The man was seized from custody on the way to jail, and the case survives in a single five-line item in the Donaldsonville Chief of March 12, 1881.

episodes.title: Killing of Fred Ludeling
episodes.summary: The killing of Fred Ludeling was the fatal shooting of Fred L. Ludeling, son of former Louisiana chief justice John T. Ludeling, and the wounding of his cousin Frank Dinkgrave on the neighboring Stubbs place on Bayou DeSiard, near Monroe in Ouachita Parish, on March 17, 1881. It followed a dispute over moving a Black family from the Stubbs place to the Ludeling place, and the four men tried for the murder were acquitted. Northern Republican papers called it a political assassination, while the Monroe press treated it as a personal quarrel between two planters.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching in Chippewa County, Wisconsin
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching in Chippewa County, Wisconsin, was an attempt by a crowd in that county to lynch an unnamed young man, who escaped from them, at some time before April 1881. It is known only from a news brief on the Wisconsin House of Representatives' rejection of a bill to restore the death penalty, which named the attempt as the origin of that effort.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joe Barnes, Vance Brandt and Julia Brandt
episodes.summary: The lynching of Joe Barnes, Vance Brandt and Julia Brandt was the hanging of three young Black people by a crowd of white and Black residents near Salem, Clarendon County, South Carolina, on or about December 8, 1880. The three were accused of killing Mrs. Thomas Kennedy, a young white woman, while robbing her house, and were hanged after the crowd voted against handing them to the courts. The Charleston News and Courier's account ran across the country, and South Carolina papers cited the case for months as a justified lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dave Spearman and Sam Fair
episodes.summary: The lynching of Dave Spearman and Sam Fair was the killing of two young Black farm laborers by a crowd near Prosperity, Newberry County, South Carolina, on January 19, 1881. Accused of assaulting and killing Bessie Werts, a white farmer's daughter, they were taken from the town guard house; Spearman was shot at a pine tree before dawn, and Fair, wounded and recaptured, was hanged at midday. The story ran in papers across the country, and the Charleston News and Courier declared that the lynchers' action "needs no apology."

episodes.title: Lynching of John J. Moore
episodes.summary: The lynching of John J. Moore took place on June 17, 1879, when an armed band took Moore, a white man, from the custody of the Spartanburg County, South Carolina, sheriff and hanged him near the spot where a young white woman's body had been found. Moore had been jailed on suspicion of the rape and murder of Frances Woodward, and he denied his guilt before a crowd of about 600. Papers outside the state noted that the man lynched was white, and a Spartanburg grand jury later declined to condemn the lynchers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Willie Johns
episodes.summary: The lynching of Willie Johns was the shooting of a young man accused of robbing and burning a store in Coffee County, Georgia, whose body was found at Indian Ford shortly before April 5, 1881. Johns had been placed in the custody of five men; two of them told a coroner's inquest that armed men had taken him from them, and the jury found that he died at the hands of "an unknown party or parties." A Georgia weekly reported the killing as a lynching, and an Atlanta dispatch carried it to Northern papers under headlines such as "Mob Law in Georgia" and "Lynched by Fiends."

episodes.title: Killing of Jourique and Sanchez and the El Paso street shooting
episodes.doubt: inventory difference: MWT lists Janrequez and Sanchez as lynched; papers report a shooting by Americans over land
episodes.summary: The killing of Jourique and Sanchez was the fatal shooting of two young Mexican men by Americans in a dispute over land near El Paso, Texas, on or about April 13, 1881. The next evening, while the bodies lay in El Paso awaiting an inquest, a quarrel over the armed Mexicans who had come for them turned into a street shooting in which a policeman and two other men were killed. Wire dispatches carried the two shootings across the United States, often under headlines about wholesale killing in Texas.

episodes.title: Hanging of Gibbs and Coleman at Hickman
episodes.summary: The hanging of Gibbs and Coleman was a night attack at Hickman, Kentucky, around 1 January 1881, in which a band hung two Black men suspected of arson to a tree until they were nearly dead. Both survived, and Black residents sought federal protection and warrants against what the Hickman Courier called a "ku klux squad."

episodes.title: Ku-klux raid on Henry Miller
episodes.summary: The Ku-klux raid on Henry Miller was a night attack in January 1881 on the house of Miller, a Black man, near Murfreesboro in Rutherford County, Tennessee, by a band of masked men who meant to whip him for alleged arson. Miller fired on the band and escaped, and one of the raiders, a man named Newman, was killed. Most papers reported that Miller shot Newman, while the New-York Tribune said an inquest found Newman was shot by one of his own companions.

episodes.title: Prairie Ridge mock hanging
episodes.summary: The Prairie Ridge mock hanging was a staged lynching on a Thursday night in early January 1881, about three miles west of Prairie Ridge in Saline County, Missouri, carried out by a masked band by arrangement with Sheriff John Cason. The band pretended to hang a willing participant, Jasper Smith, then put a rope around the neck of Thos. Barnes, a prisoner accused of burglary, until he confessed; no one was hurt.

episodes.title: Lynching of James B. Brown
episodes.summary: The lynching of James B. Brown took place in early January 1881 at Lake Providence, East Carroll Parish, Louisiana, when a group of men broke open the parish jail, took out Brown, who was held on a charge of murdering the town's city marshal, and hanged him. A coroner's jury was later reported to believe he had been shot and beaten to death before he reached the scaffold. The killing was carried by wire across the country, and several north Louisiana weeklies condemned it as the murder of a prisoner in the hands of the law.

episodes.title: Lynching of Victor Mirando
episodes.summary: The lynching of Victor Mirando was the hanging of a youth of about sixteen, described as Mexican, by six masked men near Wilmington in Los Angeles County, California, in January 1881. Accused of assaulting a girl on her way to Sunday school, he was taken from the two men who had arrested him and hanged to a willow tree, and a coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of persons unknown. The Los Angeles Herald used the case to ask whether the county was returning to vigilance justice, and a wire dispatch carried it to papers across the country.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dave Ramsey
episodes.summary: The lynching of Dave Ramsey was the killing of a Black man by a mob at or near Marianna, Lee County, Arkansas, in January 1881, after he was accused of assaulting the young daughter of C. H. Banks, a local official called the sheriff in some reports. Accounts agree that he was riddled with bullets without trial but differ on whether he was taken from the jail or caught in a pursuit, and on whether he was also hanged. The story ran as a short wire item in papers from Georgia to Minnesota, several of which headlined it as just or speedy punishment.

episodes.title: Wheeling gas works strike
episodes.summary: The Wheeling gas works strike was a work stoppage in January 1881 in which white stokers and chargers at the Gas Works in Wheeling, West Virginia, refused to work after a Black fireman was hired and were replaced by Black workers. No violence was reported, and a rumor that the strikers would interfere with the works came to nothing. The city's two dailies treated it mainly as a dispute over why the men struck, argued in signed cards into early February.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Mike Rourke
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Mike Rourke took place on January 14, 1881, at Tombstone, Arizona Territory, when a mob tried to hang Rourke, a young man arrested for shooting P. Schneider, chief engineer of the Tombstone Mill and Mining Company, at nearby Charleston. Officers kept the prisoner from the crowd and took him under armed guard to the jail at Tucson, where he awaited examination and from which he escaped in April. The Omaha Daily Bee instead reported that the killer, "John Call," was taken from jail and hanged by a mob.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Scott
episodes.summary: The lynching of George Scott took place at Brazil, Indiana, on the night of December 11-12, 1880, when masked men took Scott from the Clay county jail and hanged him from a tree beside it. Scott, described in the press as 'a half-breed Indian and negro', was being held on a charge of assaulting the wife of his employer. No one was reported arrested, and the story ran as a brief wire item in papers across the country for more than a month.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Lucinda Fowlkes
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Lucinda Fowlkes took place near Keysville, Charlotte County, Virginia, in January 1881, after Fowlkes, a Black woman, was accused of killing her husband, Wilson Fowlkes, with an axe and throwing his body into a well. January dispatches said Black neighbors would have visited "summary justice" on her but for the intervention of white residents, and she was jailed for trial instead. She was convicted of first-degree murder in the Lunenburg County Court in February and hanged privately at Lunenburg Courthouse on April 22, 1881.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joseph Daroche
episodes.summary: The lynching of Joseph Daroche took place in Bodie, California, at about 1 a.m. on January 17, 1881, when a vigilance committee took him from the town jail and hanged him where he was accused of shooting the miner Thomas H. Treloar three days earlier. It followed his escape, recapture and a preliminary examination, and some 500 men reportedly watched. Wire dispatches carried the story nationally under headlines such as "Judge Lynch at Bodie," and Nevada papers followed the town's quarrel over vigilante rule for weeks.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sharp McNut
episodes.summary: The lynching of Sharp McNut took place at Star City, Arkansas, around midnight on January 18, 1881, when an armed, masked mob of about one hundred men took him from the town jail and shot him to death. McNut was being held on a charge of murdering Dr. E. C. G. Anderson. Papers in Louisiana and Tennessee carried the news; neither states his race.

episodes.title: Killing of Noah Anderson
episodes.summary: The killing of Noah Anderson was the fatal shooting of a farmer near Carlisle, Kentucky, by masked men who forced the door of his home on the night of January 18, 1881. Anderson died almost at once, and his fifteen-year-old son Samuel, who went to his aid, was reported killed by the wire and fatally wounded by a Carlisle correspondent. The wire story, copied widely within days, said the men had come to punish Anderson for mistreating his wife.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Robert Garnes
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Robert Garnes took place near Plain City and at Marysville, Ohio, on January 18, 1881, when crowds threatened to lynch Garnes, a Black farm hand arrested for a triple murder. Officers kept him from the crowds and slipped him into the Union County jail by a back entrance, and he was later indicted and convicted of second-degree murder.

episodes.title: Hamburg shooting and threatened lynching of Harry Hackett
episodes.summary: The Hamburg shooting and threatened lynching of Harry Hackett took place on the afternoon of Thursday, January 13, 1881, in Hamburg, South Carolina, when Hackett, a Black man, fired at a white man named Damm after a quarrel and the bullet struck and mortally wounded Damm's wife. Hackett escaped, reportedly across the river to Augusta, Georgia, and South Carolina papers reported that a party was hunting him and that he would be lynched if caught. No report of his capture or fate appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Moscow, Tennessee, shooting and rescue of James Pettit
episodes.summary: The Moscow, Tennessee, shooting and rescue of James Pettit was a January 1881 episode in which Charles Smith and James Pettit were accused of trying to outrage a fifteen-year-old girl at Moscow and shooting her brother, a Black stranger, as he defended her. Both men escaped custody, Pettit with the help of two masked men, and the papers disagreed on whether the brother died.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of fire suspects at Russellville, Indiana
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of fire suspects at Russellville, Indiana, followed an incendiary fire on the night of Wednesday, January 19, 1881, that burned the town's entire business district. The men accused of setting the fire, called "fire bugs," were captured and, according to a telegraph brief, "narrowly escaped lynching." The episode is known from a single sentence in the Omaha Daily Bee, which gave no names, numbers, or race for the accused.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Abe Twiggs
episodes.doubt: Georgia report says the story was false and Twiggs alive
episodes.summary: The reported lynching of Abe Twiggs was the killing, according to an Augusta wire dispatch, of a Black man in Burke County, Georgia, on the night of Thursday, January 27, 1881, by lynchers believed to be Black. Twiggs had testified against his two brothers in a murder trial, and the dispatch tied his death to anger over that testimony. The story ran in brief across the country, but three days after it appeared the Savannah Morning News called it a false report and said Twiggs had been seen alive.

episodes.title: Lynching of Matias Salmon
episodes.summary: The lynching of Matias Salmon was the hanging of a Mexican man accused of murder by a vigilance committee or mob at Grantsville, Nevada, on the night of Saturday, January 29, 1881. Salmon had been arrested for killing a miner the day before, and he was taken from the officers holding him and hanged from the framework of a windmill. A brief telegraphic dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, while Nevada and California papers printed longer accounts that approved of the hanging.

episodes.title: Killing of George Engart
episodes.summary: The killing of George Engart was the death of a man at a dance at Roanoke, Missouri, on the night of Saturday, January 29, 1881, at the hands of a deputy constable, Add Cross. Known only from a one-sentence St. Louis wire dispatch, the killing ran as a crime brief in papers from West Virginia to California in early February.

episodes.title: Lynching of California Joe, Miguel Barrera and Escolástico Perea
episodes.summary: The lynching of California Joe, Miguel Barrera and Escolástico Perea took place in Albuquerque, New Mexico Territory, on the night of January 31, 1881, when armed men took the three Mexican prisoners from the county jail and hanged them from its portal. The men had been arrested for the murder of Colonel Charles Potter of the United States Geological Survey, the stepson of a former governor of Rhode Island, and wire dispatches carried the news nationally within two days.

episodes.title: Reported shooting of two men at San Marcial, New Mexico (1881)
episodes.summary: The reported shooting of two men at San Marcial was a killing, said to have happened in New Mexico Territory in about January 1881, in which townspeople were reported to have shot two "desperadoes" to death in a saloon. The only account came from a traveler interviewed by the Leadville Herald, and it was reprinted in papers across the country as a frontier curiosity. A New Mexico paper, the Las Vegas Morning Gazette, said no one there knew of the affair and gave the story no credence.

episodes.title: Rumored lynching of Frank Thomas
episodes.doubt: local paper withdrew the lynching report a week later
episodes.summary: The rumored lynching of Frank Thomas was the reported seizure of a young Black man accused of horse theft near Haynesville, Claiborne Parish, Louisiana, shortly before 5 January 1881, which the local Claiborne Guardian first reported as a lynching and then withdrew. A week after its first report, the Guardian said Thomas had met its editor on the street "alive and well." Two other Louisiana papers nonetheless carried the lynching story later in January, one of them adding that masked men had hanged him to a tree and praising the act.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Anton Kloefel
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Anton Kloefel took place at Big Creek, near Weissport in Carbon County, Pennsylvania, on January 2, 1881, when a crowd called for hanging a New York bakery clerk who had just been arrested for shooting his wife. The constable lodged him safely in the Mauch Chunk jail, and within two weeks a jury acquitted him of manslaughter after evidence that the shooting was unintentional. The case drew notice because it followed a lynching in neighboring Northampton County, and a Lancaster paper used it as an argument against mob law.

episodes.title: Lynching of Doyral Bryant
episodes.doubt: hanging reported as rumor, denied and repeated; body not recovered
episodes.summary: The lynching of Doyral Bryant was the reported hanging of a Black horse trader from Fayetteville, North Carolina, whose body was said to have been found on a tree between Fayetteville and Clinton in January 1881. Papers described the killers only as "parties unknown" and linked the hanging to a murder of which Bryant had been acquitted seven years earlier. A Fayetteville correspondent wrote that the report had been both denied and repeated, and that only Bryant's disappearance was certain.

episodes.title: Killing of Brooks and Griffey
episodes.summary: The killing of Brooks and Griffey was the shooting of two prisoners in James County, Tennessee, in January 1881, held on suspicion of murdering a farmer, Henry Yarnell. Rifle shots fired at night into the shop where they were held killed both men, and a widely reprinted dispatch blamed friends of Yarnell. In June 1881 a grand jury indicted three of the men who had guarded them, all relatives of Yarnell, but no report of a trial was found.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Miller
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of John Miller took place at Havana, Mason County, Illinois, in mid-January 1881, when townspeople prepared to lynch Miller after his arrest on an accusation that he had killed a young child. Guards placed over him kept the crowd away, and no violence against him was reported. The case drew notice chiefly for the accusation itself, which the Canton Register called one of the most horrible in the history of crime.

episodes.title: Lynching of horse thieves at Bernalillo, New Mexico
episodes.summary: The lynching of horse thieves at Bernalillo, New Mexico, took place in the first days of January 1881, when two men accused of horse theft, whose names were not given, were lynched in the town. The case reached the press outside the territory through a single Kansas brief and a passing mention in a later wire dispatch, and no report gave the race of the men killed.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Major Hicks
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Major Hicks was an effort by an armed crowd from Ludlow, Kentucky, to take Hicks, a young Black man held in the Covington jail on a charge of murdering Henry Williams, on the night of December 17, 1880. Covington's marshal refused to give up the prisoner, and the crowd broke up after a few shots were fired, with no one reported hurt. Hicks was later convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death, and three leaders of the mob were sentenced to jail terms and fines.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Cummins
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of John Cummins was an episode in Licking County, Ohio, in January 1881, when residents of Newark talked of lynching a farmer accused of torturing his seven-year-old son. No mob action against him was reported; he was bound over by a justice, tried in June, and fined $75. Papers across the country carried the case because of the nature of the punishment, and one later item described him as having been "almost lynched."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of McCarthy by Fort Concho soldiers
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of McCarthy by Fort Concho soldiers took place on the night of February 1, 1881, when armed Black soldiers from Fort Concho, Texas, went into San Angelo to seize McCarthy, a white man accused of killing a Black cavalryman, William Watkins. They surrounded a hotel and held the sheriff, but McCarthy had been hidden, and they returned when an officer of the guard arrived. The wire carried the story nationally as a foiled lynching, and later Texas reports described shooting into the town and state troops sent.

episodes.title: Tarboro warehouse shooting
episodes.summary: The Tarboro warehouse shooting was the shooting of an unnamed Black man by a Tarboro, North Carolina, policeman named Winborn in Capt. Brown's warehouse on a Tuesday night in early 1881. The man was said to have been stealing meat, and the only known account, a one-line item from the Tarboro Southerner, does not say whether he survived.

episodes.title: Killing of John Randolph
episodes.summary: The killing of John Randolph was the fatal stabbing of a Black man during a row at a frolic at Tobe Duke's farm in Jackson County, Georgia, on the night of Tuesday, 1 February 1881. Three brothers named Hemphill were said to have killed Randolph and gravely wounded a second man, John Tate, and two of them were arrested. The killing drew only brief notices, one in a Georgia weekly and one in an Atlanta dispatch printed in Nebraska.

episodes.title: Lynching of the Tarno brothers
episodes.summary: The lynching of the Tarno brothers was the reported hanging of three white men by a masked mob at Augusta, Arkansas, in the early hours of February 3, 1881, after they were jailed on a charge of attempting to assault a young white woman. Wire reports said the mob took the men from the jail, hanged them across the river and threw their bodies into the water, and the story ran in papers from Virginia to Dakota Territory. A later report said the prisoners were only whipped and released.

episodes.title: Lynching of Albert Williams
episodes.summary: The lynching of Albert Williams took place near Columbus, Texas, in the last days of January or the first days of February 1881, when three masked men took Williams, a Black man arrested for horse stealing, from the man who had arrested him and killed him. His body was found with his hands tied and his skull broken, and a warrant was issued for suspected parties. Wire briefs carried the killing across the country as the lynching of a horse thief.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Dock Wright
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Dock Wright took place at Museville, Pittsylvania County, Virginia, on February 5, 1881, when a crowd of citizens sought to lynch a Black man arrested for clubbing a white man, J. C. Arthur, to death at a justice's trial. According to the wire report from Richmond, the citizens were restrained only 'with great difficulty', and a guard of ten armed men took the prisoners to the county jail. Wright was later convicted of murder and hanged legally at Chatham on March 31, 1882.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Savage and Howard James
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Charles Savage and Howard James took place in Madison, Florida, in February 1881, after the two Black men were arrested for shooting Frank P. Patterson, a young lawyer, in the Madison court house on February 8 during testimony in a contested congressional election. Whites threatened to lynch the prisoners while Black residents armed to protect them, and militia guarded the jail until the men were moved to Tallahassee. The papers treated the affair as a partisan matter, and in August 1882 the two men, by then convicted and granted a new trial, were shot dead by a mob at Madison.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of the Laprade murder suspects at Springfield, Tennessee
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of the Laprade murder suspects at Springfield, Tennessee, took place on the night of February 14, 1881, when a mob of about twenty-five mounted men forced a door of the town jail intending to lynch Black prisoners brought there that day for trial. The mob dispersed after Judge Joe Stark and Attorney General B. D. Bell promised an immediate trial without a change of venue, and militia from Nashville arrived at midnight. The reprieve lasted four days: on February 18 a mob of about two hundred men took five of the prisoners from the sheriff and hanged them from the court house.

episodes.title: Killing of Sampson Hunter
episodes.summary: The killing of Sampson Hunter was the shooting of a Black man by James Orso, a white justice of the peace, who came with three men to arrest him at Escatawpa, Washington County, Alabama, on the night of February 12, 1881. Hunter resisted with an ax, was shot, and died the next morning. A jury of inquiry heard the evidence, and Orso was reported at home awaiting arrest.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John and Cicero Poe
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of John and Cicero Poe was a series of efforts in February 1881 by crowds at Winchester, Franklin County, Tennessee, to seize two brothers held on a charge of murdering a young man named Baker. Militia sent by the governor guarded the prisoners and on February 19 took them to Nashville past an armed crowd, and no one was killed. The episode ran in wire reports nationwide and set off an editorial dispute in Tennessee over mob rule in Franklin County.

episodes.title: Killing of Tom Johnson
episodes.summary: The killing of Tom Johnson was the shooting of a young Black man by four masked men at a home near Joiner's store in Clay County in February 1881. Black residents charged two sons of a local man, Joe Joiner, and two other young men with the crime, but a coroner's jury found that Johnson died at the hands of unknown parties.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Anthony Duffy and Bill Murphy
episodes.doubt: local reports say Duffy and Murphy escaped
episodes.summary: The reported lynching of Anthony Duffy and Bill Murphy refers to newspaper reports that two Black men who had testified for the State in the Laprade murder trial at Springfield, Tennessee, were hanged by a mob on the night of February 18–19, 1881. The reports followed the lynching of their five co-defendants from the Springfield court house that night and spread across the country as a one-line Nashville dispatch. Within days other dispatches said the two had not been caught and had escaped, so whether they were killed remains unsettled in the coverage.

episodes.title: Bloodhound pursuit of Tom Brounell and Bob Riching
episodes.summary: The bloodhound pursuit of Tom Brounell and Bob Riching took place on the night of February 20, 1881, when a mounted party with five bloodhounds chased the two Black men down the Brunson turnpike near Brunson's, South Carolina. The dogs threw the men to the ground after a three-mile chase, and they were arrested and jailed on a charge of store robbery. Papers in Illinois and Virginia reprinted the story as an "exciting chase," and at least one comment column mocked it as a revival of slave hunting.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Samuel Ewing
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Samuel Ewing took place on the night of Tuesday, February 22, 1881, in the eastern part of Bartholomew County, Indiana, when a masked and armed mob seized him and hanged him until he was nearly dead. The mob was trying to force him to confess to poisoning a doctor's horses, but it got no confession and left him alive. A short dispatch from Columbus, Indiana, carried the story to papers from New York to Mississippi.

episodes.title: Lynching of Faustine Guitterro
episodes.summary: The lynching of Faustine Guitterro was the hanging of a man accused of taking part in the murder of Colonel Charles Potter, whom vigilantes took from the jail at Albuquerque, New Mexico, in late February 1881. Guitterro had been brought in by a sheriff's posse only the night before, according to the wire reports. Papers noted that he was the fourth person put to death without trial for the Potter killing, after three men lynched at the same jail a month earlier.

episodes.title: Beating of Wemer by regulators near Pilot Grove
episodes.summary: The beating of Wemer by regulators near Pilot Grove was an attack in Cooper County, Missouri, in February 1881, in which 'improvised regulators' seized a German youth accused of ravishing an eight-year-old girl and beat him nearly to death. They also lashed his father, and the only known account, in the Sedalia Weekly Bazoo, presented the beating as deserved but partial punishment.

episodes.title: Torture of Joe Harris
episodes.summary: The torture of Joe Harris was a series of extralegal attacks in 1880 and 1881 on a prisoner at Rogersville, Hawkins County, Tennessee, accused of the Marble Hall double murder, including a hanging in which the rope broke. Crowds sought to lynch Harris after his arrest, but the sheriff persuaded them to let the law take its course, and Harris was later tried, convicted and legally hanged near Rogersville on November 25, 1881. A Bristol dispatch reported that the torture drew no public censure, which it attributed to local feeling over the murders.

episodes.title: Napoleon shooting of Walter G. Drury by Robert K. Scott
episodes.summary: The Napoleon shooting of Walter G. Drury by Robert K. Scott took place early on 25 December 1880, when Scott, a former Governor of South Carolina living in Napoleon, Ohio, shot and killed Drury, a young drugstore clerk, in a dispute over Scott's drunken son. Scott was charged with murder, and talk of lynching in the town led the sheriff to keep him under militia guard and then move him to the jail at Defiance. Papers across the country carried the story because of Scott's prominence as a Reconstruction governor, and one later item said he had "narrowly escaped lynching."

episodes.title: Mob assault on Mr. Love, Somerset, Kentucky
episodes.summary: The mob assault on Mr. Love was an attack in or near Somerset, Kentucky, reported in January 1881, in which a mob led by Love's wife chased him and left him hanging head downward from a tree. Love survived after a preacher cut him down about two hours later, almost frozen. The episode is known only from a short, unsigned paragraph that white newspapers in at least ten states reprinted as a curiosity about how Somerset treated "faithless husbands."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jack Byrd
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Jack Byrd was a failed effort to lynch a man accused of attempting to outrage a young lady in Rockingham County, Virginia, some time before February 1881. Byrd escaped, was convicted, and was received at the state penitentiary in Richmond on about February 24, 1881. The episode is known only from a single brief in the Richmond Daily Dispatch, which treated it as a passing detail in a report of his arrival at the prison.

episodes.title: Lynching of Granville Harrell
episodes.summary: The lynching of Granville Harrell was the hanging of a Black man by a mob near Raymond, Hinds County, Mississippi, on the night of December 18, 1880. Harrell was accused of killing his employer, David Simmons, a white Jackson meat-market keeper, with an ax two days earlier, and the sheriff had moved him to Raymond to keep him from a mob. A coroner's jury found that 75 to 100 unknown men had taken him from the jail and exonerated the officers. Mississippi papers reported the case within a week, and a short wire item carried it to papers from Louisiana to Wisconsin.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Andrew Beal
episodes.doubt: manhunt and threats only; capture or death never reported
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Andrew Beal followed the killing of Henry Speers, a white locomotive engineer, at Franklin, Missouri, on Christmas Eve 1880, when Beal, a young Black man, was accused of cutting Speers's throat with a razor. Parties of citizens hunted Beal, and newspapers called his pursuers a lynching party. No report of his capture or fate appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Killing of Antonio Maria Baca
episodes.summary: The killing of Antonio Maria Baca was the fatal shooting of a prisoner held by an armed citizens' committee of safety at Socorro, New Mexico Territory, on the night of December 28-29, 1880. The committee had seized Baca as a hostage and named him as one of the men wanted for the murder of A. M. Conkling, editor of the Socorro Sun, and a guard shot him dead after, by the guards' account, he fired a revolver and wounded another guard. Papers carried the shooting as part of a feared armed conflict between the "Americans" of Socorro and a "powerful and numerous Mexican family."

episodes.title: Mob assault on John Dove
episodes.summary: The mob assault on John Dove took place near Fawbush, in the county around Somerset, Kentucky, around the end of December 1880, when a mob of fifty men dragged Dove from his house almost naked and hanged him by the heels. He was found almost dead, and the dispatches doubted he would recover. The story ran first as crime news and then, weeks later, as a widely reprinted joke about "faithless husbands."

episodes.title: Red Men attack on Edward Davis, Roane County, West Virginia
episodes.summary: The Red Men attack on Edward Davis was a night raid in late December 1880 in which a regulator band known as the Red Men, Vigilantes or Regulators burned the house of a farmer named Davis on Spring Creek, Roane County, West Virginia, then whipped him and cut off both his ears. Davis shot and killed the band's leader during the attack and survived his injuries. Papers across the region carried the story as the worst of a string of "outrages" by the band, though the two dispatches disagreed over who had been killed.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sam and John Campbell
episodes.summary: The lynching of Sam and John Campbell took place about midnight on December 23-24, 1880, when a party of men took the two young Black brothers from the jail at Munfordville, Hart County, Kentucky, and hanged them from a tree. The brothers had been arrested that day, accused of beating and robbing John A. Gardner, a prominent Hart County citizen styled "Esquire," who lived about a mile from Rowlett's Station. The story ran within days in papers from Connecticut to Texas and Minnesota, usually under headlines naming the victims only as "negroes."

episodes.title: Lynching of Dan Smith
episodes.summary: The lynching of Dan Smith took place at Pulaski, Tennessee, on December 2, 1880, when a crowd seized Smith, a Black man, from the Giles County court room minutes after he was sentenced to twenty-one years in the penitentiary and hanged him from a bridge. Smith had been accused of assaulting a young white girl, and the sheriff had earlier sent him to Nashville to keep him from crowds. The case was widely reported because the mob overpowered the sheriff and his posse to take a prisoner who had already been sentenced.

episodes.title: Monroe County, Mississippi, stake burning (1880)
episodes.summary: The Monroe County stake burning was the killing of an unnamed man, one of two lodgers who gave the name Miller, by a crowd that burned him at a stake in northern Monroe County, Mississippi, in December 1880. He was accused of chloroforming, robbing and burning to death a young farmer, Brown Riding, with his wife and two-year-old daughter. Tupelo dispatches spread the story nationally, and northern editors argued over whether the burning was fitting punishment or murder.

episodes.title: Springfield courthouse lynching (1881)
episodes.doubt: known only from reward notices; race, number and manner not reported
episodes.summary: The Springfield courthouse lynching was the hanging of five Black men on trial for the murder of farmer L. S. Laprade, seized from the sheriff by about 200 armed men at the courthouse in Springfield, Robertson County, Tennessee, on the night of February 18, 1881. The prisoners were taken just after the judge charged the jury, and the Tennessee Senate condemned it unanimously the next day. Governor Hawkins later offered a reward for the lynchers, first $500 and then $5,000.
